c11a2ab7.content:
# Process Rule: Wheat Brown Rust (Puccinia triticina)

**Trigger**: Orange-yellow uredinia (pustules) on upper leaf surface of wheat, possibly with yellow halos.

## Step 1 — Confirm Diagnosis
- Identify orange-yellow pustules on leaf upper surface (uredinia of Puccinia triticina)
- Check for yellow halos around pustules
- Distinguish from stripe rust (yellow pustules in rows) and stem rust (dark red-brown, on stems)
- **gateway_decision**: set diagnosis = 'Brown Rust / Puccinia triticina'

## Step 2 — Assess Severity
- LOW (<15% leaf area): monitor, scout every 5 days
- MEDIUM (15–40% leaf area): fungicide application warranted
- HIGH (>40% leaf area): urgent fungicide application

## Step 3 — Weather Check Gateway
<<decision>>
- If temperature 15–22°C AND relative humidity >80%: weather_check = YES (favorable for spread)
- If temperature >30°C or dry conditions: weather_check = NO (unfavorable, monitor only)
<<if yes>>
  Proceed to Step 4 — apply fungicide
<<if no>>
  Monitor every 5 days, reassess if weather changes
<<end>>

## Step 4 — Fungicide Application
- LOW severity: Tebuconazole 250 g/L, dose 0.4–0.6 L/ha, apply early morning
- MEDIUM severity: Tebuconazole 250 g/L, dose 0.6–0.9 L/ha, apply early morning
- HIGH severity: Propiconazole 250 EC, dose 0.8–1.0 L/ha, apply immediately
- Use get_treatment_protocol to confirm product and calculate_dosage for field area
- Respect PHI (pre-harvest interval) of 35 days for Tebuconazole

## Step 5 — Follow-up
- Scout 7–10 days after application
- Should_escalate = false unless >40% canopy affected AND no fungicide response

# Process Rule: Tomato Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans)

**Trigger**: Water-soaked brown-black lesions on tomato leaves with white sporulation on leaf underside under humid conditions.

## Step 1 — Confirm Diagnosis
- Water-soaked lesions expanding rapidly, turning brown-black
- White cottony sporulation on lower leaf surface in humid conditions
- Dark cankers on stems; firm brown rot on fruits
- **gateway_decision**: set diagnosis = 'Late Blight / Phytophthora infestans'

## Step 2 — Weather Check Gateway
<<decision>>
- If temperature 10–20°C AND leaf wetness >10 hours: weather_check = YES (high risk)
- If temperature >28°C or dry: weather_check = NO (lower immediate risk)
<<if yes>>
  Proceed to Step 3 — emergency fungicide application
<<if no>>
  Preventive application, monitor every 3 days
<<end>>

## Step 3 — Severity Branch Gateway
<<decision>>
- If >30% plants symptomatic: severity_branch = YES (high severity — emergency)
- If <30% plants: severity_branch = NO (moderate — standard protocol)
<<if yes>>
  Apply cymoxanil + mancozeb at maximum dose (3 kg/ha), remove heavily infected plants
<<if no>>
  Apply cymoxanil 2.0–2.5 kg/ha or metalaxyl 0.5–1.0 kg/ha, repeat every 7 days
<<end>>

## Step 4 — Cultural Controls
- Stop overhead irrigation immediately; switch to drip or base watering
- Remove and destroy infected plant material (do not compost)
- Improve air circulation
- Use get_weather to confirm current conditions
- Use get_treatment_protocol for product selection and calculate_dosage

## Step 5 — Follow-up
- Inspect every 3–4 days
- Should_escalate = false unless >50% crop loss or systemic stem infection

8fee5b4c.content:
# Process Rule: Olive Fruit Fly (Bactrocera oleae)

**Trigger**: Oviposition stings (small dark puncture marks) on olive fruits, larval tunneling inside flesh, premature fruit drop, secondary rot.

## Step 1 — Confirm Diagnosis
- Inspect for oviposition stings: small dark puncture marks on olive skin
- Cut symptomatic fruit: look for larval galleries/tunneling in flesh
- Check for adult fly activity with yellow sticky traps
- **gateway_decision**: set diagnosis = 'Olive Fruit Fly / Bactrocera oleae'

## Step 2 — Assess Infestation Level
- Sample 50 fruits per block, count infested
- LOW: <5% infested fruits
- MEDIUM: 5–20% infested fruits
- HIGH: >20% infested fruits

## Step 3 — Infestation Threshold Gateway
<<decision>>
- If infestation >5% infested fruits: infestation_threshold = YES (above economic threshold)
- If infestation <=5%: infestation_threshold = NO (below threshold — mass trapping only)
<<if yes>>
  Proceed to Step 4 — insecticide intervention
<<if no>>
  Deploy protein bait traps (ammonium acetate + yeast), monitor weekly
<<end>>

## Step 4 — Weather Check Gateway
<<decision>>
- If temperature 15–30°C: weather_check = YES (optimal for spray efficacy)
- If temperature >35°C or <10°C: weather_check = NO (delay spray, continue trapping)
<<if yes>>
  Proceed to Step 5 — spray application
<<if no>>
  Deploy/maintain traps, reassess when temperature normalises
<<end>>

## Step 5 — Harvest Proximity Gateway
<<decision>>
- If harvest within 21 days: harvest_proximity = YES (use short-PHI product)
- If harvest >21 days away: harvest_proximity = NO (standard product)
<<if yes>>
  Apply Spinosad (PHI 7 days), dose 0.3 L/ha, early morning or evening
<<if no>>
  Apply Deltamethrin (PHI 28 days), dose 0.2–0.3 L/ha; or Dimethoate for high pressure
<<end>>

## Step 6 — Cultural Controls
- Collect and destroy fallen infested fruit daily (break life cycle)
- Prune heavily infested branches
- Use get_weather to confirm application conditions
- Use get_treatment_protocol for product confirmation
- Use check_waiting_period to verify PHI compliance

## Step 7 — Follow-up
- Inspect traps and canopy every 3–5 days
- Escalate to HIGH severity protocol if symptomatic fruit >50% or trap catches increase >20%/week
- Should_escalate = false unless grove-wide epidemic (>30% trees severely infested)

bf20dd61.trigger: wheat fusarium head blight scab Fusarium graminearum bleached spikelets tombstone kernels mycotoxin
bf20dd61.content:
# Process Rule: Wheat Fusarium Head Blight / Scab (Fusarium graminearum)

**Trigger**: Premature bleaching/whitening of individual spikelets or entire wheat heads at anthesis; pink-orange sporodochia at spikelet base; shriveled tombstone kernels.

## Step 1 — Confirm Diagnosis
- Bleached spikelets on otherwise green heads (partial head blight)
- Pink-orange spore masses at spikelet base under wet conditions
- Shriveled, chalky kernels at grain fill stage
- **gateway_decision**: set diagnosis = 'Fusarium Head Blight / Fusarium graminearum'

## Step 2 — Weather Check Gateway
<<decision>>
- If temperature 20–25°C AND humid/rainy during anthesis (GS 60–69): weather_check = YES
- If dry conditions during flowering or temperature <15°C: weather_check = NO
<<if yes>>
  HIGH risk — proceed to Step 3
<<if no>>
  LOWER risk — monitor, apply fungicide only if symptoms appear
<<end>>

## Step 3 — Timing Critical Gateway
<<decision>>
- If wheat currently at anthesis (GS 60–69, 50% head emergence): timing_critical = YES (optimal window)
- If tillering or grain fill stage: timing_critical = NO (application less effective)
<<if yes>>
  Apply fungicide immediately — this is the most critical window
<<if no>>
  Document timing constraint; note reduced efficacy in report
<<end>>

## Step 4 — Mycotoxin Risk Gateway
<<decision>>
- If susceptible variety AND high disease pressure (>25% heads symptomatic): mycotoxin_risk = YES
- Otherwise: mycotoxin_risk = NO
<<if yes>>
  Use prothioconazole + tebuconazole at full dose (1.5 L/ha) — maximum mycotoxin reduction
<<if no>>
  Standard dose: Tebuconazole 250 g/L at 1.0–1.25 L/ha
<<end>>

## Step 5 — Fungicide Application
- LOW: Tebuconazole 250 g/L, 0.8–1.0 L/ha at anthesis
- MEDIUM: Metconazole + Tebuconazole, 1.0–1.25 L/ha, repeat in 7 days
- HIGH: Prothioconazole + Tebuconazole, 1.25–1.5 L/ha, immediate
- Apply with hollow-cone nozzle aimed at heads
- Use get_weather for current conditions, get_treatment_protocol for product, calculate_dosage
- Use check_waiting_period — PHI Tebuconazole: 35 days

## Step 6 — Follow-up
- Monitor mycotoxin levels at harvest (DON threshold: 1.25 ppm EU)
- Should_escalate = true if >50% heads symptomatic AND grain filling already initiated (irreversible yield loss)

744eb99e.trigger: citrus greening HLB huanglongbing Liberibacter blotchy mottle asymmetric yellowing psyllid Diaphorina citri
744eb99e.content:
# Process Rule: Citrus Greening / HLB (Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus)

**Trigger**: Blotchy mottling on citrus leaves not following vein patterns (asymmetric); lopsided small fruits; yellow shoots; presence of psyllid vector (Diaphorina citri).

## Step 1 — Confirm Diagnosis
- Blotchy mottle: asymmetric yellowing NOT following leaf veins (unlike nutritional deficiency)
- Lopsided fruits with bitter juice and underdeveloped seeds
- Yellow flush shoots with twig/branch dieback
- Psyllid nymphs or adults on new growth
- **gateway_decision**: set diagnosis = 'Citrus Greening / HLB / Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus'

## Step 2 — Confirmation Test Gateway
<<decision>>
- If PCR test or field diagnostic kit confirms Liberibacter: confirmation_test = YES
- If test negative or pending: confirmation_test = NO
<<if yes>>
  Confirmed HLB — proceed to Step 3 eradication protocol
<<if no>>
  Treat as nutritional deficiency (Zn/Mn foliar spray), retest in 30 days
<<end>>

## Step 3 — Tree Removal Gateway
<<decision>>
- If disease incidence >30% in block: tree_removal = YES (remove infected + buffer trees)
- If incidence <30%: tree_removal = NO (intensive vector suppression)
<<if yes>>
  Remove infected trees + 2-tree buffer; immediate psyllid suppression in surrounding blocks
  Notify local plant health authority
<<if no>>
  Intensive psyllid vector suppression program (Step 4)
<<end>>

## Step 4 — Vector Pressure Gateway
<<decision>>
- If psyllid >1 nymph per flush shoot: vector_pressure = YES (high pressure)
- If psyllid <=1 nymph per flush: vector_pressure = NO (low pressure)
<<if yes>>
  Apply Spirotetramat (systemic) + Dimethoate (contact), dose 1.0–1.5 L/ha
  Repeat every 3 weeks during new flush periods
<<if no>>
  Preventive: Imidacloprid soil drench or foliar, 0.3–0.5 L/ha at flush emergence
<<end>>

## Step 5 — Nutritional Support
- All HLB-positive trees: foliar micronutrient program (Zn, Mn, B, Cu) every 6 weeks
- Maintain optimal irrigation and fertilization to slow symptom progression
- Use get_disease_info for Liberibacter confirmed distribution in region
- Use get_treatment_protocol for current-approved psyllicide
- Use check_waiting_period for PHI compliance
- Use send_sms to notify grove owner of confirmed HLB status

## Step 6 — Follow-up
- Monitor psyllid populations monthly with yellow sticky traps
- Resample disease incidence quarterly
- Should_escalate = true if incidence spreading to adjacent blocks despite interventions

4a253487.trigger: When leaf rust (brown rust) caused by Puccinia recondita is suspected or identified in wheat, triticale, or related grasses based on symptoms of circular to slightly elliptical orange to orange-brown pustules on upper leaf surfaces and leaf sheaths.
4a253487.content:
<<trigger>>: When leaf rust (brown rust) caused by Puccinia recondita is suspected or identified in wheat, triticale, or related grasses based on symptoms of circular to slightly elliptical orange to orange-brown pustules on upper leaf surfaces and leaf sheaths.
<<steps>>:
1. Confirm presence of leaf rust by examining upper surfaces of leaves and leaf sheaths for circular or slightly elliptical pustules containing orange to orange-brown urediospores, and check for occasional infection on neck and awns.
   <<decision>>: Are pustules present with orange to orange-brown urediospores, primarily on upper leaf surfaces?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2.
     <<if no>>: Consider alternative diseases (e.g., stem rust with dark reddish brown pustules on both leaf sides, stems, and spikes; or stripe rust) and refer to diagnostic key.
2. Assess environmental conditions for disease development risk.
   <<decision>>: Is free moisture (rain, dew, or irrigation water) present on host plant surfaces and is ambient temperature near 20°C?
     <<if yes>>: Note that disease can develop rapidly; proceed to step 3.
     <<if no>>: Note that conditions are less favorable; monitor for black teliospores as plants mature or conditions change, and proceed to step 3.
3. Evaluate potential yield impact based on timing and severity of infection.
   <<decision>>: Are infections severe and occurring early in the growing season?
     <<if yes>>: Expect significant yield losses, primarily from reduced number of kernels per spike, reduced test weights, and reduced kernel quality.
     <<if no>>: Expect lower impact; continue monitoring for disease progression.
4. Implement management actions based on risk assessment.
   <<decision>>: Is disease risk high (favorable moisture and temperature, early infection, severe symptoms)?
     <<if yes>>: Apply appropriate fungicide treatment according to local recommendations, targeting successive generations of urediospores every 10-14 days under favorable conditions.
     <<if no>>: Continue field monitoring; consider resistant varieties or cultural practices for future seasons.
<<end>>

685b13eb.trigger: When monitoring wheat, barley, or triticale crops for rust and smut diseases under varying temperature and moisture conditions.
685b13eb.content:
<<trigger>>: When monitoring wheat, barley, or triticale crops for rust and smut diseases under varying temperature and moisture conditions.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess average temperature conditions for stem rust (Puccinia graminis) development.
   <<decision>>: If temperatures average about 20°C or more?
     <<if yes>>: Expect first generation of urediospores to be produced in 10-15 days; monitor for pustules and potential black teliospores as plants mature.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; moderate temperatures may delay urediospore production.
2. Assess temperature and moisture conditions for stripe rust (Puccinia striiformis) development.
   <<decision>>: If free moisture (rain or dew) occurs and temperatures range between 10-20°C?
     <<if yes>>: Expect rapid disease development; monitor for yellow to orange-yellow urediospore pustules forming narrow stripes on leaves, leaf sheaths, necks, and glumes.
     <<if no>>: If temperatures exceed 25°C, expect reduced or ceased urediospore production and possible black teliospore formation.
3. Evaluate risk of common bunt (Tilletia caries, T. foetida) or dwarf bunt (T. controversa) infection.
   <<decision>>: If cool temperatures prevail during seed germination and seedlings are emerging?
     <<if yes>>: Expect infection from dormant spores in soil or on seed; monitor for bluish-green spikes, bunt balls replacing kernels, and fetid odor after soft dough stage; note that dwarf bunt occurs in areas with prolonged snow cover and causes pronounced height reduction.
     <<if no>>: Infection risk is low; continue standard monitoring.
4. Evaluate risk of Karnal bunt (Tilletia indica) infection.
   <<decision>>: If crop is at spike emergence through grain filling stage and inoculum (teliospores) is present on or near soil surface?
     <<if yes>>: Expect wind-borne sporidia to infect floral structures; monitor for black teliospores replacing portion of endosperm in kernels post-harvest; note that barley is not affected.
     <<if no>>: Infection risk is low; continue standard monitoring.
5. Evaluate risk of loose smut (Ustilago tritici) infection.
   <<decision>>: If cool, humid conditions prolong flowering period and wind-borne teliospores are present?
     <<if yes>>: Expect infection of developing embryo; monitor for entire inflorescence (except rachis) replaced by black teliospores at flowering time; incidence usually less than 1% of spikes.
     <<if no>>: Infection risk is low; continue standard monitoring.
6. Evaluate risk of flag smut (Urocystis agropyri) infection.
   <<decision>>: If low soil moisture and cool soil temperatures prevail during kernel germination or very early seedling stage?
     <<if yes>>: Expect systemic infection; monitor for stunted plants, profuse tillering, rolled onion-type leaves, and black subepidermal strips of teliospores on leaves and leaf sheaths near heading.
     <<if no>>: Infection risk is low; continue standard monitoring.
<<end>>

2840c374.content:
<<trigger>>: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of Fusarium Leaf Blotch (Snow Mold) at late-joint to early-boot growth stage, with oval to elliptical greyish green mottled lesions that develop into large eyespot blotches with bleached centers and leaf shredding.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess environmental conditions for disease development
   <<decision>>: Are conditions cool and moist (cool, moist weather favors development)?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2
     <<if no>>: Monitor crop; disease development is unlikely under warm, dry conditions
2. Evaluate crop type and susceptibility
   <<decision>>: Is the crop durum wheat or triticale?
     <<if yes>>: High risk; proceed to step 3

9e770401.trigger: When diagnosing potential root and stem diseases in wheat or other small grain cereals in temperate regions, based on observed symptoms and field conditions.
9e770401.content:
<<trigger>>: When diagnosing potential root and stem diseases in wheat or other small grain cereals in temperate regions, based on observed symptoms and field conditions.
<<steps>>:
1. Observe symptoms on roots, stems, and leaf sheaths
   <<decision>>: Are roots and lower stems shiny black, with stunted plants and whitened stems/spikes?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2 for Take-All diagnosis
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3
2. Assess Take-All (Gaeumannomyces graminis f. sp. tritici)
   <<decision>>: Are soil temperatures cool (12-18°C), soils alkaline or nutrient deficient, and nitrate present?
     <<if yes>>: Confirm Take-All; note that early infection reduces tillers and causes sterile spikes; late infection confined to roots with less damage
     <<if no>>: Consider other diseases; proceed to step 3
3. Observe for eye-shaped lesions on lower stem internodes
   <<decision>>: Are there elliptical lesions with dark brown to greenish brown rings and straw-colored centers on lower stem, without root symptoms?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 4 for Eyespot diagnosis
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5
4. Assess Eyespot (Pseudocercosporella herpotrichoides)
   <<decision>>: Is weather cool and damp, with high humidity at soil level, and crop is fall-sown wheat?
     <<if yes>>: Confirm Eyespot; expect potential lodging, reduced kernel size/number, and tiller death
     <<if no>>: Consider other diseases; proceed to step 5
5. Observe for superficial, sharply outlined lesions on basal leaf sheaths with dark brown margins and pale centers
   <<decision>>: Are lesions superficial, with mycelia easily removed by rubbing, and roots brown and reduced?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 6 for Sharp Eyespot/Rhizoctonia Root Rot diagnosis
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 7
6. Assess Sharp Eyespot/Rhizoctonia Root Rot (Rhizoctonia solani)
   <<decision>>: Are soils dry, sandy, cool, with high humidity, and field continuously sown to cereals (especially winter wheat)?
     <<if yes>>: Confirm Rhizoctonia solani; expect stunting and reduced tillers; no major epidemics reported
     <<if no>>: Consider other diseases; proceed to step 7
7. Observe for darkening or browning of root, crown, and basal culm tissues, with white spikes before maturity
   <<decision>>: Are there darkened tissues, lodging, or pre-/post-emergence damping off?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 8 for Common Root Rot, Foot Rot, Crown Rot diagnosis
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 9
8. Assess Common Root Rot, Foot Rot, Crown Rot (Helminthosporium, Fusarium, Pythium spp.)
   <<decision>>: Are soils warm and dry with plants under stress?
     <<if yes>>: Likely Helminthosporium spp. (common root rot)
     <<if no>>: Proceed to sub-decision
       <<decision>>: Are soils cool and moist?
         <<if yes>>: Likely Fusarium spp. (root, foot, crown rot)
         <<if no>>: Likely Pythium spp. (favored by wet soils)
   <<end sub-decision>>
   Note: Positive field identification of causal agent is difficult; expect thinned stands, reduced tillers, head size, and test weights
9. Observe for white, fluffy mycelia on tissues and soil, with sclerotia on crown or near soil surface
   <<decision>>: Are there white mycelia, rotted culms/crowns/roots, white heads/spikes, and sclerotia present?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 10 for Sclerotium Wilt diagnosis
     <<if no>>: Re-evaluate symptoms or consider other diseases not covered
10. Assess Sclerotium Wilt (Southern Blight) (Corticum rolfsii)
    <<decision>>: Did infection occur early in crop cycle?
      <<if yes>>: Expect pre- or post-emergence damping off
      <<if no>>: Expect rotted culms, crowns, roots, and eventual plant death with white heads
<<end>>

e51f2a98.trigger: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of blackened spikes, water-soaked lesions, or yellow exudate, and environmental conditions or pest presence suggest a fungal, bacterial, or viral disease.
e51f2a98.content:
<<trigger>>: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of blackened spikes, water-soaked lesions, or yellow exudate, and environmental conditions or pest presence suggest a fungal, bacterial, or viral disease.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the specific symptoms on the plant (e.g., blackened spikes, water-soaked lesions on glumes or leaves, yellow exudate on spikes, distorted spikes or leaves).
   <<decision>>: Are the symptoms a blackened appearance of mature or dead spikes, with no water-soaked lesions or exudate?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2 for Black Molds (Sooty Molds) assessment.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3 for bacterial disease assessment.
2. Assess for Black Molds (Sooty Molds):
   <<decision>>: Is the crop at or near maturation, or are plants heavily infested with aphids, or have plants died prematurely, with wet or humid weather present?
     <<if yes>>: Conclude that black molds (Alternaria, Cladosporium, etc.) are likely present. Note that these are saprophytic and generally not economically important, but under humid/rainy conditions they may cause kernel discoloration (black point or smudge). No specific treatment is required unless kernel quality is a concern.
     <<if no>>: Re-evaluate symptoms; black molds are unlikely.
3. Assess for bacterial diseases based on symptom location and type:
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms narrow, water-soaked chlorotic lesions or stripes on leaves/leaf sheaths, or blackening on glumes, with possible sticky yellowish exudate?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 4 for Bacterial Black Chaff/Bacterial Stripe (Xanthomonas campestris pv. translucens).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms small, dark green, water-soaked lesions on leaves, culms, or spikes that turn dark brown to black, starting at the base of the glume, with possible whitish gray bacterial ooze under wet conditions?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 6 for Basal Glume Rot/Bacterial Leaf Blight (Pseudomonas syringae pv. atrofaciens).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 7.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms a yellow exudate on spikes (drying to white), with distorted spikes and necks emerging as a sticky mass, possibly with wrinkled or twisted early leaves?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 8 for Bacterial Spike Blight (Corynebacterium tritici).
     <<if no>>: Re-evaluate symptoms; consider viral diseases or other disorders.
4. Manage Bacterial Black Chaff/Bacterial Stripe:
   <<decision>>: Is free moisture present (rain, dew, splashing) and are temperatures warm (above 20°C)?
     <<if yes>>: Note that infection and spread are favored. The bacterium is seed-borne and persists on crop residues. No specific treatment is detailed in the document; monitor for severity. Disease rarely causes significant damage.
     <<if no>>: Conditions are less favorable; continue monitoring.
5. Manage Basal Glume Rot/Bacterial Leaf Blight:
   <<decision>>: Is there wet or humid weather, and are symptoms present on glumes, stems, or leaves?
     <<if yes>>: Note that the pathogen survives on crop debris and grass hosts, spread by splashing rain or insects, and can be seed-borne. Disease usually not economically important but frequently reported in humid areas. No specific treatment detailed.
     <<if no>>: Conditions less favorable; continue monitoring.
6. Manage Bacterial Spike Blight:
   <<decision>>: Is the crop wheat, and is the nematode Anguina tritici present in the region?
     <<if yes>>: Note that the bacteria is associated with the nematode for transmission. Disease is not economically important. No specific treatment detailed.
     <<if no>>: Transmission may be less likely; continue monitoring.
7. If symptoms do not match bacterial or fungal descriptions, consider viral diseases (e.g., Barley Yellow Dwarf) or other disorders (genetic melanism, frost damage, Septoria nodorum blotch). Note that viral identification requires vector analysis (e.g., aphids) and is not detailed further in this document.
<<end>>

c07b5b70.trigger: When a cereal crop (wheat, barley, triticale, oats, or other grasses) shows symptoms of yellowing or reddening of leaves, stunting, upright thickened stiff leaves, reduced root growth, delayed or no heading, heads that remain erect and become black and discolored during ripening, and yield reduction, and Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus (BYDV) is suspected.
c07b5b70.content:
<<trigger>>: When a cereal crop (wheat, barley, triticale, oats, or other grasses) shows symptoms of yellowing or reddening of leaves, stunting, upright thickened stiff leaves, reduced root growth, delayed or no heading, heads that remain erect and become black and discolored during ripening, and yield reduction, and Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus (BYDV) is suspected.
<<steps>>:
1. Confirm symptoms and assess disease development conditions
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms present (yellowing on wheat/barley, reddening on oats/some wheats, stunting, upright thickened stiff leaves, reduced root growth, delayed/no heading, black discolored heads during ripening) and is the temperature approximately 20°C?
     <<if yes>>: Note that symptoms typically appear approximately 14 days after infection; proceed to step 2.
     <<if no>>: Consider other causes (e.g., nutrient deficiencies, other diseases, insect damage) as symptoms may be masked or confused with other problems.
2. Identify potential aphid vectors in the field
   <<decision>>: Are aphids present, especially species such as Rhopalosiphum padi, Schizaphis graminum, R. maidis, Metopolophium dirhodum, Sitobion avenae, or Diuraphis noxia?
     <<if yes>>: Recognize that these aphids may act as vectors of BYDV; proceed to step 3.
     <<if no>>: Consider that aphid vectors may have been present earlier but are no longer visible; proceed to step 3.
3. Assess infection timing and potential yield impact
   <<decision>>: Did infection occur early in the crop cycle?
     <<if yes>>: Expect yield losses of more than 20%, and potentially much larger losses.
     <<if no>>: Yield losses may be lower, but still monitor for symptom progression.
4. Confirm diagnosis using specialized techniques
   <<decision>>: Is positive identification of BYDV required?
     <<if yes>>: Use an electron microscope and serological techniques for confirmation.
     <<if no>>: Base management on symptom observation and known presence of aphid vectors.
<<end>>

7e20e298.trigger: When stink bugs, armyworms, cutworms, stalk borers, cereal leaf beetles, thrips, Hessian flies, or wheat stem maggots are detected or suspected in cereal crops, and the user requests a management or identification protocol.
7e20e298.content:
<<trigger>>: When stink bugs, armyworms, cutworms, stalk borers, cereal leaf beetles, thrips, Hessian flies, or wheat stem maggots are detected or suspected in cereal crops, and the user requests a management or identification protocol.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the pest based on symptoms and morphology.
   <<decision>>: Is the pest a shield-shaped adult insect (approx. 60) that emits a disagreeable odor when crushed, and is feeding on developing heads or kernels?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as stink bug. Note that feeding during early stages destroys kernels, later stages shrivel grain, and may cause partial or total sterility. Overwinters as adults under dead leaves/grass; migrates to cereals in spring. Outbreaks favored by mild winters and low rainfall.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Check for defoliation, larvae chewing leaves from edges to midrib, or larvae severing the neck below the head.
   <<decision>>: Are larvae present that feed at night (or all day in damp weather), hide in soil cracks/rocks during day, and are omnivorous on grasses?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as armyworms, cutworms, or stalk borers. Note that heavy infestations can devastate large areas. Larvae may feed on leaves, heads, soil surface, roots, or inside stems.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Examine leaves for distinct longitudinal stripes and look for small (4-5 mm) beetles with black head, light brown thorax, shiny blue-green wing covers with parallel dots, or slimy yellow larvae covered with black fecal mass.
   <<decision>>: Are these symptoms present on fall-sown cereals (especially winter wheat or fall-sown spring wheat), and are hairy-leaved wheat varieties less affected?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as cereal leaf beetle (Oulema melanopa). Note one generation per year; adults feed in spring, lay yellow eggs singly or in chains covered with sticky film; pupation in soil; adults overwinter under plant debris, leaf sheaths, ears of maize, or tree bark. Yield losses of 14% to >25% possible.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Look for very small (1 mm) brown or black insects with piercing-sucking mouthparts, narrow wings, found behind flag leaf sheath, on stems, leaves, or heads, causing silver coloration on tissue.
   <<decision>>: Are these thrips present in large numbers, and is there a risk of serious damage?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as thrips. Note that heavy rains usually destroy high proportion of population; generation time very short (10+ generations/year). However, thrips rarely cause serious damage warranting control.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
5. Check for stunted plants, thin stands, lodging, reduced yield, or stems breaking before maturity. Look for small (3-4 mm) flies with black head/thorax and pinkish/yellow-brown abdomen, or reddish-brown pupae ("flag seed") behind leaf sheaths at nodes.
   <<decision>>: Are reddish oblong eggs laid in rows on upper leaf surfaces, or white legless larvae sucking sap behind leaf sheaths, or translucent pale green slug-like maggots present?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as Hessian fly (Mayetiola destructor). Note adults emerge in spring from overwintered pupae in straw/stubble; eggs hatch within one week; pupae are 3-5 mm, oval, flattened, tapered. Mainly pest of wheat but may attack barley, rye, other grasses. One of most destructive cereal pests; widespread outbreaks occur annually in some regions (e.g., North Africa, USA).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 6.
6. Observe for "white head" condition in tillers, especially when young tillers die in fall or early spring.
   <<decision>>: Are stems bored internally, causing tiller death and white heads?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as wheat stem maggot (Meromyza americana). Note that attack on young tillers in fall or early spring usually kills the tiller.
     <<if no>>: No specific pest identified from provided symptoms; consult additional resources.
<<end>>

2fac4c6d.trigger: When adult flies (pale green to yellow with dark stripes, ~6 mm) are observed in wheat fields, or when symptoms of premature yellowing of the head, shriveled grain, or stem girdling are detected.
2fac4c6d.content:
<<trigger>>: When adult flies (pale green to yellow with dark stripes, ~6 mm) are observed in wheat fields, or when symptoms of premature yellowing of the head, shriveled grain, or stem girdling are detected.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the pest based on symptoms and life cycle timing.
   <<decision>>: Are the symptoms premature yellowing of the head, shriveled grain, and stem lodging with larvae girdling the stem base?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as sawfly (Cephus cinctus). Proceed to step 2 for sawfly-specific management.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3 for other pest identification.
2. For sawfly infestation:
   <<decision>>: Is the wheat variety a solid or partially solid stem type?
     <<if yes>>: Note that these varieties are much less susceptible; continue monitoring.
     <<if no>>: Recognize that fall-sown cereals are more commonly attacked; consider cultural controls such as crop rotation or resistant varieties.
3. If symptoms are not sawfly, examine for other pests:
   <<decision>>: Are there small white eggs laid singly near the sheath of the flag leaf, with larvae burrowing into the stem and killing the upper stem and head?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as wheat stem maggot. Note that there are three generations per year (spring, summer, early autumn). Monitor infested fields where 10-15% of plants may be injured.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. If symptoms include wilting or dying patches of seedlings:
   <<decision>>: Are roots partially or completely severed, with large larvae (up to several cm long, ~1 cm thick, three pairs of legs) found in the soil?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as white grubs (May/June beetle larvae). Avoid seeding wheat into heavily infested grasslands.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
5. If seedlings show wilting/dying in rows or patches, with stems chewed just above the seed:
   <<decision>>: Are larvae present that are 20-30 mm long, smooth, hard, wire-like, with three pairs of legs, and color ranging from cream to brown?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as wireworms (click beetle larvae). Note that damage is most severe after fallow or years of grass; consider delayed planting or seed treatments.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 6.
6. If symptoms include feeding on endosperm of germinating seed, seedlings bitten off at ground level, or longitudinal stripes on leaves:
   <<decision>>: Are the pests slugs, snails, grasshoppers, or crickets?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as slugs/snails/grasshoppers/crickets. Note that damage is localized but can be severe in individual stands; monitor and apply appropriate controls.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 7.
7. If symptoms include silvery flecking on leaves, stunting, poor heading, or white discoloration:
   <<decision>>: Are very small arthropods (<1 mm) with sucking mouthparts present, possibly with webs?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as mites. Note that wheat curl mite (Eriophyes tulipae) has only two pairs of legs; treat if large numbers cause significant damage.
     <<if no>>: Re-evaluate symptoms or consult additional diagnostic resources.
<<end>>

052b1d25.trigger: When a leaf sample shows potential mite infestation but no mites are visible to the unaided eye.
052b1d25.content:
<<trigger>>: When a leaf sample shows potential mite infestation but no mites are visible to the unaided eye.
<<steps>>:
1. Hold the infested leaf over a piece of white paper folded to form a trough.
   <<decision>>: Is the leaf tapped sharply several times?
     <<if yes>>: Observe whether hundreds of mites fall onto the paper and are seen moving about.
     <<if no>>: Repeat tapping until mites are dislodged or confirm absence.
<<end>>

594781bd.trigger: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of poor growth, discoloration, or necrosis that may be due to mineral deficiencies, toxicities, or environmental stresses.
594781bd.content:
<<trigger>>: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of poor growth, discoloration, or necrosis that may be due to mineral deficiencies, toxicities, or environmental stresses.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess visual symptoms to determine if the issue is likely genetic or environmental.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms consistent with genetic conditions (melanism, genetic flecking, hybrid necrosis)?
     <<if yes>>: Note that genetic flecking does not necessarily affect yield; hybrid necrosis usually appears in early generation material and affected progeny should be eliminated. No further action required unless yield is severely affected.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Evaluate for nutrient deficiencies based on symptom location and color.
   <<decision>>: Is the plant pale green with lower leaves yellowing from tip to sheath?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect nitrogen deficiency. Apply nitrogen fertilizer as per standard agronomic practice.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Check for phosphorus deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are plants stunted with fewer shoots, pale to yellowish-red lower leaves, bluish-green leaf portions, or purple culm bases?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect phosphorus deficiency. Apply phosphorus fertilizer as per standard agronomic practice.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Check for potassium deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are internodes shortened, with dry and scorched tips and margins of lower leaves?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect potassium deficiency. Apply potassium fertilizer as per standard agronomic practice.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
5. Check for manganese deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are there grayish necrotic spots or streaks on the basal portion of the newest leaves, possibly causing kinking or twisting?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect manganese deficiency. Apply foliar manganese sulfate to alleviate deficiency.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 6.
6. Check for copper deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are young leaf tips discolored, followed by breaking and curling, or are spikes bleached, sterile, or not emerging properly?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect copper deficiency. Apply copper-containing fertilizer as per standard agronomic practice.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 7.
7. Check for aluminum toxicity.
   <<decision>>: Are roots stubby and brownish, with small leaves, shortened internodes, leaf tip death, and yellow brittle old leaves?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect aluminum toxicity associated with low soil pH. Reduce toxicity by liming the soil.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 8.
8. Check for salt stress.
   <<decision>>: Is crop growth variable within the field with barren spots, plants stunted and dark blue-green, with tip burn and firing on leaf margins?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect salt stress. Confirm with a soil test for excessive salt levels. If confirmed, manage irrigation and drainage to reduce salt buildup.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 9.
9. Check for moisture stress.
   <<decision>>: Are plants stunted with reduced tillering and root development, leaves curling/rolling during midday, or reduced spikelets/florets/grain shriveling?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect moisture stress. Ensure adequate irrigation, especially during late booting and seed set.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 10.
10. Check for heat stress.
    <<decision>>: Are symptoms of high temperature (increased development rate, reduced growth) present, often associated with moisture stress?
      <<if yes>>: Suspect heat stress. Manage irrigation and consider shading or other cooling measures if possible.
      <<if no>>: Re-evaluate symptoms or consult a specialist for further diagnosis.
<<end>>

bafeffb5.trigger: When high temperatures or frost damage is suspected in wheat crops, or when herbicide damage from 2,4-D or triazine residues is observed.
bafeffb5.content:
<<trigger>>: When high temperatures or frost damage is suspected in wheat crops, or when herbicide damage from 2,4-D or triazine residues is observed.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess the crop growth stage and environmental conditions
   <<decision>>: Is the crop in the late-boot, seed-set, flowering, or maturity stage?
     <<if yes>>: Check for high temperatures (especially if desiccating winds occur) and monitor for yield reductions due to reduced spikelets, florets, and grain filling.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Evaluate for herbicide damage symptoms
   <<decision>>: Are there signs of leaf curling, deformed spikes, or sterility?
     <<if yes>>: Determine if hormonal herbicides like 2,4-D were applied too early in the crop cycle or near anthesis; note that such damage is generally limited and seldom causes significant losses in small grain cereals.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Check for triazine residue effects
   <<decision>>: Are there symptoms of leaf bleaching followed by necrosis?
     <<if yes>>: Investigate if triazines (such as atrazine) were applied to the preceding crop; these residues can adversely affect wheat growth.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Assess for frost damage
   <<decision>>: Is there chlorosis, banding/striping on leaves or spikes, bleached white tissue, sterility, or separated peduncle epidermis?
     <<if yes>>: Determine if frost occurred, especially at flowering; note that young or newly emerged tissue and flowering parts are most susceptible, and frost can be serious if it occurs late in the crop cycle.
     <<if no>>: No action required based on this document.
<<end>>

6fe13b70.trigger: When leaf rust (brown rust) caused by Puccinia recondita is suspected or identified in wheat, triticale, or related grasses based on symptoms of circular to slightly elliptical orange to orange-brown pustules on upper leaf surfaces and leaf sheaths.
6fe13b70.content:
<<trigger>>: When leaf rust (brown rust) caused by Puccinia recondita is suspected or identified in wheat, triticale, or related grasses based on symptoms of circular to slightly elliptical orange to orange-brown pustules on upper leaf surfaces and leaf sheaths.
<<steps>>:
1. Confirm presence of leaf rust by examining plants for circular or slightly elliptical pustules containing orange to orange-brown urediospores on upper surfaces of leaves and leaf sheaths, and occasionally on the neck and awns.
   <<decision>>: Are pustules present with orange to orange-brown urediospores, smaller than stem rust pustules, and primarily on upper leaf surfaces?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2.
     <<if no>>: Consider alternative diseases (e.g., stem rust with dark reddish brown pustules on both leaf sides, stems, and spikes; or stripe rust).
2. Assess environmental conditions for disease development risk.
   <<decision>>: Is free moisture (rain, dew, or irrigation water) available on the host plant surface and is ambient temperature near 20°C?
     <<if yes>>: Note that disease can develop rapidly; successive generations of urediospores can be produced every 10-14 days if conditions remain favorable. Proceed to step 3.
     <<if no>>: Note that disease development is less favorable; as plants mature or conditions become unfavorable, black teliospores may appear. Monitor regularly.
3. Evaluate potential yield impact.
   <<decision>>: Are infections severe and occurring early in the growing season?
     <<if yes>>: Expect significant yield losses, mainly by reducing number of kernels per spike, test weights, and kernel quality. Implement management actions (e.g., fungicide application if available and appropriate).
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; light infections may not cause economically significant losses.
<<end>>

eecd68aa.trigger: When monitoring wheat, barley, or triticale crops for rust diseases (stem rust or stripe rust) and environmental conditions are favorable for disease development.
eecd68aa.content:
<<trigger>>: When monitoring wheat, barley, or triticale crops for rust diseases (stem rust or stripe rust) and environmental conditions are favorable for disease development.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess average temperature and moisture conditions for stem rust risk.
   <<decision>>: Is the average temperature about 20°C or more?
     <<if yes>>: Expect first generation of urediospores to be produced in 10-15 days; monitor for pustules and potential severe effects if infection occurs during early crop stages (reductions in tillering, grain weight/quality, possible complete crop loss).
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; moderate temperatures may still allow slower development.
2. Assess temperature and free moisture conditions for stripe rust risk.
   <<decision>>: Are temperatures between 10-20°C and is free moisture (rain or dew) present?
     <<if yes>>: Expect rapid disease development from wind-borne urediospores; monitor for yellow to orange-yellow pustules forming narrow stripes on leaves, leaf sheaths, necks, and glumes.
     <<if no>>: If temperatures are above 25°C, note that urediospore production is reduced or ceases and black teliospores may be produced; continue monitoring.
3. Evaluate crop stage and infection timing for potential severity.
   <<decision>>: Did infection occur during early crop stages?
     <<if yes>>: Anticipate severe effects including reductions in tillering, grain weight, and quality; under favorable conditions, complete crop loss can occur for stem rust.
     <<if no>>: For stripe rust, severe infections can still cause yield losses by reducing number of kernels per spike, test weights, and kernel quality; continue monitoring.
<<end>>

7bca4ada.trigger: When powdery mildew (Erysiphe graminis f. sp. tritici) is detected on wheat, with symptoms of white to pale gray powdery colonies on upper leaf surfaces and leaf sheaths.
7bca4ada.content:
<<trigger>>: When powdery mildew (Erysiphe graminis f. sp. tritici) is detected on wheat, with symptoms of white to pale gray powdery colonies on upper leaf surfaces and leaf sheaths.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess environmental conditions for disease favorability
   <<decision>>: Are temperatures between 15-22°C, cloudy conditions present, and relative humidity between 75-100%?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2; conditions are highly favorable for disease development.
     <<if no>>: Monitor regularly; disease development is less likely under current conditions.
2. Evaluate infection timing and severity
   <<decision>>: Did infection occur early in the crop cycle, and are conditions remaining favorable for development so that high infection levels are reached before heading?
     <<if yes>>: Implement fungicide treatment immediately to prevent major yield losses.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; risk of major yield loss is lower if infection occurs later or conditions are less favorable.
<<end>>

630b0097.trigger: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of Fusarium Leaf Blotch (Snow Mold) at late-joint to early-boot growth stage, with oval to elliptical greyish green mottled lesions that develop into large "eyespot" blotches with bleached or light grey centers and leaf shredding.
630b0097.content:
<<trigger>>: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of Fusarium Leaf Blotch (Snow Mold) at late-joint to early-boot growth stage, with oval to elliptical greyish green mottled lesions that develop into large "eyespot" blotches with bleached or light grey centers and leaf shredding.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess environmental conditions for disease development
   <<decision>>: Are conditions cool and moist (cool, moist weather)?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2; disease development is favored.
     <<if no>>: Monitor crop; disease development is less likely.
2. Evaluate crop type and susceptibility
   <<decision>>: Is the crop durum wheat or triticale?
     <<if yes>>: High risk; proceed to step 3 for management.
     <<if no>>: Lower risk for bread wheat or rye; oats and barley are immune; monitor as needed.
3. Determine severity of disease development
   <<decision>>: Is there evidence of complete defoliation or severe blotching?
     <<if yes>>: Expect poor grain development, shriveling, and low test weights; implement control measures (e.g., fungicide application based on local recommendations).
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; disease may not cause significant yield loss.
<<end>>

75beeea7.trigger: When assessing potential disease risks in wheat or other small grain cereals, particularly in fields with poor drainage, monocropping, or specific soil and environmental conditions.
75beeea7.content:
<<trigger>>: When assessing potential disease risks in wheat or other small grain cereals, particularly in fields with poor drainage, monocropping, or specific soil and environmental conditions.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the disease based on observed symptoms and plant parts affected.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms primarily on roots and lower stems with shiny black discoloration, and are soil temperatures cool (12-18°C) with alkaline or nutrient-deficient soils?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Take-All (Gaeumannomyces graminis f. sp. tritici). Note that nitrate enhances development; infection early in crop cycle reduces tillers and causes sterile spikes; later infections cause less damage.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Check for eye-shaped lesions on lower stem internodes with dark brown rings and straw-colored centers.
   <<decision>>: Are lesions present on lower stem internodes, with no root symptoms, and is the environment cool, damp, with high humidity at soil level?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Eyespot (Pseudocercosporella herpotrichoides). Note that wheat is most susceptible, especially winter wheat and fall-sown spring wheat; yield loss from reduced kernel size, number, and lodging.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Examine lesions on basal leaf sheaths that are superficial, sharply outlined, with dark brown margins and pale centers, and check for brown, reduced roots.
   <<decision>>: Are lesions superficial and sharply outlined on leaf sheaths, with mycelia easily rubbed off, and are conditions dry, sandy soils with cool temperatures and high humidity?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Sharp Eyespot/Rhizoctonia Root Rot (Rhizoctonia solani). Note that it is more severe in fields continuously sown to cereals, especially winter wheat.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Observe for darkening or browning of root, crown, and basal culm tissues, white spikes before maturity, or damping-off in seedlings.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms general browning of roots/crown/culm, with possible lodging or white spikes, and is identification of causal agent difficult?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Common Root Rot, Foot Rot, or Crown Rot (Helminthosporium, Fusarium, or Pythium spp.). Determine favoring conditions: warm dry soils for Helminthosporium, cool moist soils for Fusarium, wet soils for Pythium.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
5. Look for white, fluffy mycelia on plant surfaces and soil, rotted culms/crowns/roots, white heads in green crop, and sclerotia on crown or soil surface.
   <<decision>>: Are white fluffy mycelia present on diseased tissues and soil, with sclerotia visible, and does infection cause damping-off or plant death?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Sclerotium Wilt (Southern Blight) (Corticum rolfsii). Note that early infection causes damping-off; disease leads to white heads and plant death.
     <<if no>>: No specific disease identified from this document; consult further resources.
<<end>>

46b43191.trigger: When a crop shows symptoms of black molds (sooty molds) such as blackened appearance of mature or dead spikes, or when wet/humid weather occurs near crop maturation, or when plants are heavily infested with aphids, or when plants die prematurely.
46b43191.content:
<<trigger>>: When a crop shows symptoms of black molds (sooty molds) such as blackened appearance of mature or dead spikes, or when wet/humid weather occurs near crop maturation, or when plants are heavily infested with aphids, or when plants die prematurely.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess whether the crop is at or near maturation, or if plants are dead or dying.
   <<decision>>: Are wet or humid conditions present, or is there heavy aphid infestation, or have plants died prematurely?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2.
     <<if no>>: No action needed; black molds are not a disease and only invade dead or dying tissue.
2. Evaluate economic impact by checking if humid or rainy conditions are causing invasion of mature kernels.
   <<decision>>: Are mature kernels being invaded, leading to discoloration, black point, or smudge?
     <<if yes>>: Note that black molds are generally not economically important, but under these conditions they can cause kernel discoloration; monitor for quality impact.
     <<if no>>: No further action; black molds are saprophytic and not economically important.
<<end>>

c7d09612.trigger: When a cereal crop (wheat, barley, triticale, oats, or other grasses) shows symptoms of yellowing or reddening of leaves, stunting, upright thickened stiff leaves, reduced root growth, delayed or no heading, black discolored heads during ripening, and yield reduction, and Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus (BYDV) is suspected.
c7d09612.content:
<<trigger>>: When a cereal crop (wheat, barley, triticale, oats, or other grasses) shows symptoms of yellowing or reddening of leaves, stunting, upright thickened stiff leaves, reduced root growth, delayed or no heading, black discolored heads during ripening, and yield reduction, and Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus (BYDV) is suspected.
<<steps>>:
1. Confirm symptom presentation and timing
   <<decision>>: Do symptoms include yellowing (or reddening on oats/some wheats), stunting, upright thickened stiff leaves, reduced root growth, delayed or no heading, and black discolored heads during ripening?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2
     <<if no>>: Consider other causes (e.g., nutrient deficiency, other diseases, insect damage) and do not apply BYDV rule
2. Assess environmental conditions and infection timing
   <<decision>>: Is the temperature approximately 20°C and have symptoms appeared approximately 14 days after potential infection?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 3
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; disease development may be less favorable at other temperatures
3. Evaluate aphid vector presence
   <<decision>>: Are aphid species present, including Rhopalosiphum padi, Schizaphis graminum, R. maidis, Metopoliphium dirhodum, Sitobion avenae, or Diuraphis noxia?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 4
     <<if no>>: Consider other causes; BYDV transmission requires aphid vectors
4. Determine infection timing relative to crop cycle
   <<decision>>: Did infection occur early in the crop cycle?
     <<if yes>>: Expect potential yield losses of more than 20%; implement management actions (e.g., aphid control, resistant cultivars if available)
     <<if no>>: Expect lower yield impact; continue monitoring for symptom progression and aphid activity
<<end>>

f96dc64a.trigger: When stink bugs, armyworms, cutworms, stalk borers, cereal leaf beetles, thrips, Hessian flies, or wheat stem maggots are detected or suspected in cereal crops, and the user requests a management or identification protocol.
f96dc64a.content:
<<trigger>>: When stink bugs, armyworms, cutworms, stalk borers, cereal leaf beetles, thrips, Hessian flies, or wheat stem maggots are detected or suspected in cereal crops, and the user requests a management or identification protocol.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the pest based on symptoms and morphology.
   <<decision>>: Is the pest a shield-shaped adult insect that emits a disagreeable odor when crushed and causes kernel destruction, shriveled grain, or sterility?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as stink bug. Note that mild winters and low rainfall favor outbreaks. Proceed to step 2 for stink bug management.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 1b.
1b. <<decision>>: Is the primary symptom defoliation (chewed leaves from edges to midrib, or severed heads), with larvae feeding at night or early morning, and found in soil cracks or under rocks during the day?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as armyworm, cutworm, or stalk borer. Note that heavy infestations can devastate large areas. Proceed to step 2 for these pests.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 1c.
1c. <<decision>>: Are there distinct longitudinal stripes on leaves, with adult beetles 4-5 mm long (black head, light brown thorax, shiny blue-green wing covers) and larvae appearing as slimy, black masses due to fecal material?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as cereal leaf beetle (Oulema melanopa). Note that fall-sown cereals and wheats with non-hairy leaves are more affected. Proceed to step 2 for cereal leaf beetle.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 1d.
1d. <<decision>>: Are insects very small (1 mm long), brown or black, with piercing-sucking mouthparts, found behind the flag leaf sheath, and causing silver coloration on tissue?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as thrips. Note that heavy rains usually destroy a high proportion of the population, and serious damage is rare. Proceed to step 2 for thrips.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 1e.
1e. <<decision>>: Is there stunting, thin stands, lodging, or broken stems, with larvae sucking sap behind leaf sheaths, and reddish-brown pupae resembling flax seeds found at nodes?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as Hessian fly (Mayetiola destructor). Note that it is one of the most destructive cereal pests, recurring annually in some regions. Proceed to step 2 for Hessian fly.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 1f.
1f. <<decision>>: Do young tillers die in fall or early spring, with infested plants showing a "white head" condition typical of stem-boring insects?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as wheat stem maggot (Meromyza americana). Proceed to step 2 for wheat stem maggot.
     <<if no>>: Pest not clearly identified from this document. Advise user to consult local extension service for further diagnosis.

2. Assess the severity and need for control.
   <<decision>>: For stink bugs, are insect densities high, weather conditions favorable (mild winter, low rainfall), and crop in early development stages (kernel destruction risk) or later stages (grain shriveling risk)?
     <<if yes>>: Recommend monitoring and potential control due to reduced baking quality losses.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; losses are variable.
   <<decision>>: For armyworms, cutworms, or stalk borers, is infestation heavy (e.g., larvae severing heads or causing widespread defoliation)?
     <<if yes>>: Recommend immediate control measures as these can devastate large areas.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; damage is sporadic.
   <<decision>>: For cereal leaf beetle, is infestation on winter wheat or fall-sown spring wheat, with yield loss potential of 14% to over 25%?
     <<if yes>>: Recommend control measures to prevent significant yield loss.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; hairy-leaved wheats are less affected.
   <<decision>>: For thrips, are numbers large enough to cause silver coloration on tissue?
     <<if yes>>: Consider control only if damage is severe; note that heavy rains may naturally reduce population.
     <<if no>>: No action needed; thrips rarely cause serious damage.
   <<decision>>: For Hessian fly, is infestation occurring during jointing or causing stunting, thin stands, or lodging?
     <<if yes>>: Recommend control measures; this is one of the most destructive pests.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; outbreaks can be widespread.
   <<decision>>: For wheat stem maggot, are young tillers dying in fall or early spring?
     <<if yes>>: Recommend control measures to prevent white head condition.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring.

<<end>>

40a8fc66.trigger: When a leaf sample needs to be assessed for mite infestation using a visual inspection method.

53e7f1d9.trigger: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of poor growth, discoloration, or necrosis that may be due to mineral deficiencies, toxicities, or environmental stresses.
53e7f1d9.content:
<<trigger>>: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of poor growth, discoloration, or necrosis that may be due to mineral deficiencies, toxicities, or environmental stresses.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess visual symptoms to determine if the issue is likely genetic or environmental.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms consistent with genetic conditions (melanism, genetic flecking, hybrid necrosis)?
     <<if yes>>: Note that genetic flecking does not necessarily affect yield; hybrid necrosis usually appears in early generation material and affected progeny should be eliminated. No further action required unless yield is affected.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Evaluate for nutrient deficiencies based on symptom location and color.
   <<decision>>: Is the plant pale green with lower leaves yellowing from tip to sheath?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect nitrogen deficiency. Apply nitrogen fertilizer as needed.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Check for phosphorus deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are plants stunted with fewer shoots, or are lower leaves pale to yellowish red with possible bluish-green leaf portions and purple culm bases?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect phosphorus deficiency. Apply phosphorus fertilizer as needed.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Check for potassium deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are internodes shortened, with lower leaf tips and margins dry and scorched?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect potassium deficiency. Apply potassium fertilizer as needed.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
5. Check for manganese deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are grayish necrotic spots or streaks on the basal portion of newest leaves, possibly causing kinking or twisting?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect manganese deficiency, especially in calcareous, sandy, or high organic matter soils. Apply foliar manganese sulfate.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 6.
6. Check for copper deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are young leaf tips discolored, followed by breaking and curling, or are spikes bleached, sterile, or not emerging properly?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect copper deficiency. Apply copper fertilizer as needed.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 7.
7. Assess for aluminum toxicity.
   <<decision>>: Are roots stubby and brownish, with small leaves, shortened internodes, leaf tip death, and yellow brittle old leaves?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect aluminum toxicity associated with low soil pH. Reduce toxicity by liming.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 8.
8. Assess for salt stress.
   <<decision>>: Is crop growth variable within the field (barren spots), with stunted, dark blue-green plants showing tip burn and leaf margin firing?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect salt stress. Confirm with soil test. If excessive, manage irrigation and drainage.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 9.
9. Assess for moisture stress.
   <<decision>>: Are plants stunted with reduced tillering and root development, or leaves curling/rolling during midday, or reduced spikelets/florets, or grain shrivelling, or sterility during late booting/seed set?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect moisture stress. Ensure adequate irrigation or rainfed management.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 10.
10. Assess for heat stress.
    <<decision>>: Are symptoms of high temperature (increased development rate, reduced growth) present, often associated with moisture stress?
      <<if yes>>: Manage heat stress through irrigation, shading, or timing of planting.
      <<if no>>: Re-evaluate for other causes or consult further diagnostic resources.
<<end>>

70682d9a.trigger: When high temperatures or frost damage is suspected in wheat crops, or when herbicide phytotoxicity symptoms are observed.
70682d9a.content:
<<trigger>>: When high temperatures or frost damage is suspected in wheat crops, or when herbicide phytotoxicity symptoms are observed.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the type of damage based on symptoms and timing.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms leaf curling, deformed spikes, or sterility occurring near anthesis?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute damage to hormonal herbicide (e.g., 2,4-D) application too early or near anthesis; note that deformations seldom cause significant losses in small grain cereals.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Check for leaf bleaching followed by necrosis.
   <<decision>>: Are leaves bleached and then necrotic?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute damage to triazine herbicide residues (e.g., atrazine) from previous crop; note that damage results from excessive amounts, wrong growth stage, or wrong species.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Assess for frost damage symptoms.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms chlorosis, banding/striping on leaves or spikes, bleached white tissue, sterility at flowering, or separated peduncle epidermis?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute damage to frost; note that young/newly emerged tissue and flowering parts are most susceptible, and frost can be serious if late in crop cycle.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Evaluate for high temperature damage.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms reduced spikelets, florets, or grain filling, especially during late-boot or seed-set stages, or plant death from protein denaturation?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute damage to high temperatures; note that flowering to maturity period often coincides with hot, dry weather, and desiccating winds with high temperatures cause major yield reductions.
     <<if no>>: Conclude that damage is not clearly identified from the document; consider other causes.
<<end>>

08fed77a.trigger: When leaf rust (brown rust) caused by Puccinia recondita is suspected in wheat, triticale, or related grasses based on field symptoms of circular to slightly elliptical orange to orange-brown pustules on upper leaf surfaces and leaf sheaths.
08fed77a.content:
<<trigger>>: When leaf rust (brown rust) caused by Puccinia recondita is suspected in wheat, triticale, or related grasses based on field symptoms of circular to slightly elliptical orange to orange-brown pustules on upper leaf surfaces and leaf sheaths.
<<steps>>:
1. Confirm presence of leaf rust by examining plants for circular or slightly elliptical pustules, smaller than stem rust pustules, containing orange to orange-brown urediospores, primarily on upper surfaces of leaves and leaf sheaths, and occasionally on the neck and awns.
   <<decision>>: Are pustules dark reddish brown, occurring on both sides of leaves, stems, and spikes, with a ragged and torn appearance?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect stem rust (Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici) instead; refer to stem rust management protocol.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Assess environmental conditions for disease development risk.
   <<decision>>: Is free moisture (rain, dew, or irrigation water) present on plant surfaces and ambient temperature near 20°C?
     <<if yes>>: Note that disease can develop rapidly; successive generations of urediospores can be produced every 10-14 days under favorable conditions. Proceed to step 3.
     <<if no>>: Note that disease development is less favorable; monitor conditions and re-evaluate if free moisture and temperatures near 20°C occur.
3. Evaluate potential yield impact.
   <<decision>>: Are infections severe and occurring early in the growing season?
     <<if yes>>: Expect significant yield losses, primarily from reduced number of kernels per spike, reduced test weights, and reduced kernel quality. Proceed to step 4.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; early light infections typically develop from wind-borne urediospores and may not cause significant losses.
4. Implement management actions.
   <<decision>>: Is the crop at a growth stage where fungicide application is feasible and economically justified?
     <<if yes>>: Apply appropriate fungicide according to local recommendations for leaf rust control, targeting conditions with free moisture and temperatures near 20°C.
     <<if no>>: Rely on cultural practices (e.g., resistant varieties, crop rotation, timely planting) and continue monitoring for disease progression.
<<end>>

46bf3182.trigger: When monitoring wheat, barley, or triticale crops for rust diseases (stem rust or stripe rust) and environmental conditions are favorable for disease development.
46bf3182.content:
<<trigger>>: When monitoring wheat, barley, or triticale crops for rust diseases (stem rust or stripe rust) and environmental conditions are favorable for disease development.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess average temperature and moisture conditions for stem rust risk
   <<decision>>: Is the average temperature about 20°C or more?
     <<if yes>>: Expect first generation of urediospores to be produced in 10-15 days; monitor for pustules containing reddish-brown urediospores on stems and leaves.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; moderate temperatures may still allow slower development.
2. Assess temperature and free moisture conditions for stripe rust risk
   <<decision>>: Is free moisture (rain or dew) present AND temperatures between 10-20°C?
     <<if yes>>: Expect rapid disease development; monitor for yellow to orange-yellow urediospores forming narrow stripes on leaves, leaf sheaths, necks, and glumes.
     <<if no>>: If temperatures are above 25°C, note that urediospore production is reduced or ceases and black teliospores may be produced; continue monitoring.
3. Evaluate crop stage and infection timing for severity assessment
   <<decision>>: Did infection occur during early crop stages?
     <<if yes>>: Anticipate severe effects including reductions in tillering, grain weight, and quality; under favorable conditions, complete crop loss can occur.
     <<if no>>: Later infection may cause yield losses mainly by reducing number of kernels per spike, test weights, and kernel quality.
<<end>>

2d6fbc8c.content:
<<trigger>>: When powdery mildew (Erysiphe graminis f. sp. tritici) is detected on wheat, with symptoms of white to pale gray powdery colonies on upper leaf surfaces and leaf sheaths, and conditions are cool (15-22°C), cloudy, and humid (75-100% relative humidity).

3b21efba.trigger: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of Fusarium Leaf Blotch (Snow Mold) at late-joint to early-boot growth stage, with oval to elliptical greyish green mottled lesions that develop into large eyespot blotches with bleached centers and leaf shredding.
3b21efba.content:
<<trigger>>: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of Fusarium Leaf Blotch (Snow Mold) at late-joint to early-boot growth stage, with oval to elliptical greyish green mottled lesions that develop into large eyespot blotches with bleached centers and leaf shredding.

     <<if yes>>: Note that these are more affected than bread wheat or rye; proceed to step 4
     <<if no>>: If crop is oats or barley, disease is unlikely (immune); if bread wheat or rye, risk is lower than durum wheat or triticale; proceed to step 4 with adjusted risk assessment

6138598b.trigger: When diagnosing potential root and stem diseases in wheat or other small grain cereals in temperate regions, based on observed symptoms and field conditions.
6138598b.content:
<<trigger>>: When diagnosing potential root and stem diseases in wheat or other small grain cereals in temperate regions, based on observed symptoms and field conditions.
<<steps>>:
1. Observe symptoms on roots, stems, and leaf sheaths.
   <<decision>>: Are roots and lower stems shiny black, with stunted plants and whitened stems/spikes?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2 for Take-All (Gaeumannomyces graminis f. sp. tritici).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
2. Assess Take-All conditions.
   <<decision>>: Are soil temperatures cool (12-18°C), soils alkaline or nutrient deficient, and nitrate present, with infection occurring in fall or early spring?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Take-All; note that early infection reduces tillers and causes sterile spikes, and disease is widespread in monocropped areas with liming or minimum tillage.
     <<if no>>: Consider later-season infection causing less damage, confined to roots.
3. Observe for eye-shaped lesions on lower stem internodes.
   <<decision>>: Are there elliptical lesions with dark brown to greenish brown rings and straw-colored centers on lower stem, with possible stem breakage near ground?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 4 for Eyespot (Pseudocercosporella herpotrichoides).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
4. Assess Eyespot conditions.
   <<decision>>: Is weather cool and damp, with high humidity at soil level, and is the crop fall-sown wheat?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Eyespot; note that symptoms do not appear on roots, and yield loss results from reduced kernel size/number and lodging.
     <<if no>>: Consider other diseases.
5. Observe for superficial, sharply outlined lesions on basal leaf sheaths with dark brown margins and pale centers, and brown, reduced roots.
   <<decision>>: Are lesions superficial with easily removable mycelia, and are soils dry, sandy, and cool with high humidity?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Sharp Eyespot/Rhizoctonia Root Rot (Rhizoctonia solani); note it is more severe in continuous winter wheat.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 6.
6. Observe for darkening or browning of root, crown, and basal culm tissues, with possible white spikes before maturity.
   <<decision>>: Are there signs of pre- or post-emergence damping off, or lodging?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 7 for Common Root Rot, Foot Rot, or Crown Rot (Helminthosporium, Fusarium, or Pythium spp.).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 8.
7. Assess conditions for Common Root Rot, Foot Rot, or Crown Rot.
   <<decision>>: Are soils warm and dry with plants under stress?
     <<if yes>>: Likely Helminthosporium spp. (common root rot).
     <<if no>>: Are soils cool and moist?
       <<if yes>>: Likely Fusarium spp. (foot and crown rot).
       <<if no>>: Are soils wet?
         <<if yes>>: Likely Pythium spp.
         <<if no>>: Positive field identification difficult; consider multiple pathogens.
8. Observe for white, fluffy mycelia on diseased tissues, rotted culms/crowns/roots, white heads in green crop, and sclerotia on crown or soil surface.
   <<decision>>: Are sclerotia present and infection causing damping off or plant death?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Sclerotium Wilt (Southern Blight) caused by Corticum rolfsii (Sclerotium rolfsii).
     <<if no>>: Re-evaluate symptoms or consider other pathogens not detailed.
<<end>>

54071213.trigger: When a crop shows symptoms of black molds (sooty molds) such as blackened appearance of mature or dead spikes, or when wet/humid weather occurs near crop maturation, or when plants are heavily infested with aphids, or when plants die prematurely.
54071213.content:

1003a0db.content:
<<trigger>>: When adult flies (pale green to yellow with dark stripes, ~6 mm) are observed in wheat fields, or when symptoms of premature yellowing of the head, shriveled grain, or stem girdling are detected.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the pest type based on symptoms and field examination.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms premature yellowing of the head, shriveled grain, and stem lodging with stem girdling at the base?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2 for sawfly (Cephus cinctus) management.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3 for wheat stem maggot management.
2. Manage sawfly infestation.
   <<decision>>: Is the wheat variety a solid or partially solid stem type?
     <<if yes>>: Note that these varieties are less susceptible; continue monitoring.
     <<if no>>: Recognize that fall-sown cereals are more commonly attacked; consider cultural controls (e.g., crop rotation, residue management) as sawflies produce one generation per year and larvae overwinter in straw.
3. Manage wheat stem maggot infestation.
   <<decision>>: Is the current generation spring, summer, or early autumn?
     <<if yes>>: Note that there are three generations per year; larvae overwinter in cereal plants or grasses. Monitor for small white eggs laid one per stem near the sheath of the flag leaf.
     <<if no>>: Continue regular scouting.
4. For other pests (white grubs, wireworms, slugs, snails, grasshoppers, crickets, mites), examine soil and plants for specific signs.
   <<decision>>: Are there patches of wilting or dying seedlings with roots severed or chewed?
     <<if yes>>: Examine soil for white grubs (larvae with three pairs of legs, up to several cm long) or wireworms (20-30 mm, tough, wire-like, three pairs of legs). If white grubs found, note that damage is non-uniform and plants may survive if roots not completely destroyed. If wireworms found, note that damage is most severe after fallow or years of grass.
     <<if no>>: Check for slugs/snails (feeding on endosperm, biting seedlings at ground level, chewing longitudinal stripes on leaves), grasshoppers/crickets (damage similar to cutworms/armyworms), or mites (silvery flecking on leaves, stunting, poor heading, white discoloration; wheat curl mite has only two pairs of legs).
<<end>>

   <<decision>>: Are these symptoms present?

119c10b1.trigger: When high temperatures or frost damage are observed in wheat crops, or when herbicide phytotoxicity is suspected.
