a9fba6e4.trigger: When stink bugs, armyworms, cutworms, stalk borers, cereal leaf beetles, thrips, Hessian flies, or wheat stem maggots are detected or suspected in cereal crops, and the user requests a pest management response.
a9fba6e4.content:
<<trigger>>: When stink bugs, armyworms, cutworms, stalk borers, cereal leaf beetles, thrips, Hessian flies, or wheat stem maggots are detected or suspected in cereal crops, and the user requests a pest management response.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the pest species based on symptoms and morphology described in the document.
   <<decision>>: Is the pest a stink bug (shield-shaped body, 60, disagreeable odor when crushed)?
     <<if yes>>: Assess that feeding on developing heads may cause partial or total sterility; note that mild winters and low rainfall favor outbreaks; proceed to step 2 for stink bug management.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to next pest identification.
   <<decision>>: Is the pest an armyworm, cutworm, or stalk borer (symptoms: defoliation, larvae chewing leaves from edges to midrib, severing neck below head, feeding on roots or inside stem)?
     <<if yes>>: Note that larvae feed at night or early morning, may feed all day in damp weather; heavy infestations can devastate large areas; proceed to step 2 for these pests.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to next pest identification.
   <<decision>>: Is the pest a cereal leaf beetle (Oulema melanopa, adults 4-5 mm, black head, light brown thorax, shiny blue-green wing covers with parallel dots; larvae yellow turning to slimy black mass; symptom: longitudinal stripes on leaves)?
     <<if yes>>: Note that yield losses of 14% to >25% can occur in winter wheat and fall-sown spring wheat; proceed to step 2 for cereal leaf beetle management.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to next pest identification.
   <<decision>>: Is the pest thrips (1 mm long, brown or black, piercing-sucking mouthparts, found behind flag leaf sheath, silver coloration on tissue)?
     <<if yes>>: Note that thrips rarely cause serious damage and infestations usually do not warrant control; heavy rains destroy high proportion of population; proceed to step 2 for thrips management.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to next pest identification.
   <<decision>>: Is the pest Hessian fly (Mayetiola destructor, adults 3-4 mm, black head and thorax, pinkish/yellow-brown abdomen; larvae suck sap; symptoms: stunting, thin stands, lodging, reduced yield, stems break prior to maturity)?
     <<if yes>>: Note that this is one of the most destructive cereal pests, recurring annually in some regions; proceed to step 2 for Hessian fly management.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to next pest identification.
   <<decision>>: Is the pest wheat stem maggot (Meromyza americana, symptoms: young tillers die, "white head" condition)?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2 for wheat stem maggot management.
     <<if no>>: Report that the pest does not match any described in the document; advise further expert consultation.

2. Determine the appropriate management action based on pest and infestation level.
   <<decision>>: For stink bugs, is the infestation occurring during early kernel development or later stages?
     <<if yes>>: Note that early feeding destroys the kernel, later feeding shrivels grain; advise monitoring density and weather conditions (mild winters, low rainfall favor outbreaks); no specific control dosage or product is provided in the document.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; no action specified.
   <<decision>>: For armyworms, cutworms, or stalk borers, is the infestation heavy (severe defoliation or larvae severing heads)?
     <<if yes>>: Note that these pests can devastate large areas; advise monitoring at night or early morning; no specific control dosage or product is provided in the document.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; no action specified.
   <<decision>>: For cereal leaf beetle, is the crop winter wheat or fall-sown spring wheat with visible longitudinal stripes on leaves?
     <<if yes>>: Note that yield losses of 14% to >25% can occur; advise monitoring adults and larvae; no specific control dosage or product is provided in the document.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; no action specified.
   <<decision>>: For thrips, is the infestation causing silver coloration on tissue and present in large numbers?
     <<if yes>>: Note that thrips rarely cause serious damage and infestations usually do not warrant control; heavy rains will destroy a high proportion; no specific control dosage or product is provided in the document.
     <<if no>>: No action needed; thrips are typically not a concern.
   <<decision>>: For Hessian fly, is infestation occurring during jointing or causing stunting, thin stands, lodging?
     <<if yes>>: Note that this is one of the most destructive pests; advise monitoring for reddish-brown pupae ("flag seed") behind leaf sheaths at nodes; no specific control dosage or product is provided in the document.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; no action specified.
   <<decision>>: For wheat stem maggot, are young tillers attacked in fall or early spring showing "white head" condition?
     <<if yes>>: Note that attacked tillers usually die; no specific control dosage or product is provided in the document.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; no action specified.

<<end>>

e07af3b0.trigger: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of poor growth, discoloration, or necrosis that may be due to mineral deficiencies, toxicities, or environmental stresses.
e07af3b0.content:
<<trigger>>: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of poor growth, discoloration, or necrosis that may be due to mineral deficiencies, toxicities, or environmental stresses.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess visual symptoms and field conditions to determine the likely cause.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms pale green lower leaves with yellowing from tip to sheath, possibly followed by necrosis?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as nitrogen deficiency; apply nitrogen fertilizer as per standard agronomic practice.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Evaluate for phosphorus deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are plants stunted with fewer shoots, pale to yellowish red leaves starting from lower leaves, bluish-green leaf portions, purple culm bases, or small heads?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as phosphorus deficiency; apply phosphorus fertilizer as per standard agronomic practice.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Evaluate for potassium deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are internodes shortened, with dry and scorched tips and margins of lower leaves?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as potassium deficiency; apply potassium fertilizer as per standard agronomic practice.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Evaluate for manganese deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are there grayish necrotic spots or streaks on the basal portion of the newest leaves, possibly causing kinking or twisting?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as manganese deficiency; apply foliar applications of manganese sulfate.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
5. Evaluate for copper deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are young leaf tips discolored, followed by breaking and curling of leaves, or bleached and sterile spikes, or spikes not emerging properly?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as copper deficiency; apply copper fertilizer as per standard agronomic practice.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 6.
6. Evaluate for aluminum toxicity.
   <<decision>>: Are roots stubby and brownish, with small leaves, shortened and thickened internodes, leaf tip death, and old leaves yellow and brittle?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as aluminum toxicity; reduce toxicity by liming to raise soil pH.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 7.
7. Evaluate for salt stress.
   <<decision>>: Is there variability in crop growth within the field (barren spots), with stunted, dark blue-green plants showing tip burn and firing on leaf margins?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as salt stress; confirm with a soil test for excessive salt levels.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 8.
8. Evaluate for moisture stress.
   <<decision>>: Are plants stunted with reduced tillering and root development, curling/rolling of leaves during midday, reduced spikelets/florets, grain shrivelling, or sterility during late booting/seed set?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as moisture stress; manage irrigation or water conservation practices.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 9.
9. Evaluate for heat stress.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms associated with high temperatures (increased development rate, reduced growth rate) and difficult to separate from moisture stress?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as heat stress; manage through shading, irrigation, or timing of planting.
     <<if no>>: Consider genetic disorders (e.g., genetic flecking, hybrid necrosis) or other non-nutrient/environmental causes.
<<end>>

9e77ea44.trigger: When monitoring wheat, barley, or triticale crops for rust or smut diseases under varying temperature and moisture conditions.
9e77ea44.content:
<<trigger>>: When monitoring wheat, barley, or triticale crops for rust or smut diseases under varying temperature and moisture conditions.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the disease based on symptom observation
   <<decision>>: Are pustules present on leaves, forming narrow stripes with yellow to orange-yellow urediospores?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to stripe rust management (step 2)
     <<if no>>: Check for other symptoms
       <<decision>>: Are masses of black teliospores replacing kernels or forming bunt balls with a fetid odor?
         <<if yes>>: Proceed to bunt or smut identification (step 3)
         <<if no>>: Check for stem rust symptoms: reddish-brown pustules on stems or leaves, with black teliospores on mature plants
           <<decision>>: Are stem rust symptoms present?
             <<if yes>>: Proceed to stem rust management (step 4)
             <<if no>>: Continue monitoring for other diseases (flag smut, loose smut) based on symptom descriptions

2. Manage stripe rust (Puccinia striiformis)
   <<decision>>: Is free moisture (rain or dew) present and temperature between 10-20°C?
     <<if yes>>: Expect rapid disease development; apply fungicide treatment if infection is severe to reduce yield losses (reduced kernels per spike, test weight, kernel quality)
     <<if no>>: If temperature is above 25°C, urediospore production is reduced or ceases; monitor for black teliospores but disease spread is limited

3. Manage bunt or smut diseases
   <<decision>>: Are bunt balls the same size and shape as kernels (common bunt) or more spherical (dwarf bunt), with bluish-green spikes and slight or pronounced height reduction?
     <<if yes>>: For common or dwarf bunt (Tilletia spp.), use chemical seed treatments to prevent infection; infection favored by cool temperatures during germination; ensure susceptible cultivars are not grown without treatment
     <<if no>>: Check for Karnal bunt (Tilletia indica): only a few kernels per spike affected, black teliospores replace part of endosperm, fetid odor when crushed
       <<decision>>: Is Karnal bunt suspected?
         <<if yes>>: Note that yield loss is minimal but disease is quarantine-relevant; inspect harvested grain visually; manage as seed- or soil-borne floral infecting disease with environmental conditions from spike emergence through grain filling
         <<if no>>: Check for loose smut (Ustilago tritici): entire inflorescence replaced by black teliospores, leaving bare rachis
           <<decision>>: Is loose smut present?
             <<if yes>>: Infection favored by cool, humid conditions prolonging flowering; yield loss depends on spike incidence (usually <1%, rarely >30%); manage by using resistant cultivars or seed treatments
             <<if no>>: Check for flag smut (Urocystis agropyri): black teliospore strips under epidermis, stunted plants, rolled leaves, onion-type appearance
               <<decision>>: Is flag smut present?
                 <<if yes>>: Infection favored by low soil moisture and cool soil temperatures; manage with seed treatments and resistant bread wheat cultivars

4. Manage stem rust (Puccinia graminis)
   <<decision>>: Do temperatures average about 20°C or more?
     <<if yes>>: First generation of urediospores will be produced in 10-15 days; apply fungicide if infection occurs during early crop stages to prevent severe reductions in tillering, grain weight, and quality; under favorable conditions, complete crop loss can occur
     <<if no>>: If moderate temperatures prevail, monitor for urediospore production; as plants mature, black teliospores may appear; manage alternate hosts (Berberis and Mahonia spp.) to reduce inoculum

<<end>>

1. Assess infection timing and severity
   <<decision>>: Is infection occurring early in the crop cycle and conditions remain favorable for development so that high infection levels may be reached before heading?
     <<if yes>>: Initiate fungicide application to prevent major yield losses; monitor for black spherical fruiting structures (cleistothecia) developing in mycelia.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; no immediate treatment required as powdery mildew generally is not an economically important disease unless early infection and favorable conditions persist.
<<end>>

041d9d1b.trigger: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of Fusarium Leaf Blotch (Snow Mold) at late-joint to early-boot growth stage, with oval to elliptical greyish green mottled lesions that develop into large eyespot blotches with bleached or light grey centers and leaf shredding.
041d9d1b.content:
<<trigger>>: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of Fusarium Leaf Blotch (Snow Mold) at late-joint to early-boot growth stage, with oval to elliptical greyish green mottled lesions that develop into large eyespot blotches with bleached or light grey centers and leaf shredding.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess environmental conditions for disease development
   <<decision>>: Are conditions cool and moist (cool, moist weather)?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2
     <<if no>>: Monitor crop; disease development is not favored under current conditions
2. Evaluate crop debris management
   <<decision>>: Is crop debris present on or near the soil surface?
     <<if yes>>: Recognize that spores are produced on this debris and can be transmitted by wind or splashing rain; proceed to step 3
     <<if no>>: Risk of primary inoculum is reduced; continue monitoring
3. Determine host susceptibility
   <<decision>>: Is the crop durum wheat or triticale?
     <<if yes>>: Note that these are more affected than bread wheat or rye; proceed to step 4
     <<if no>>: If crop is oats or barley, note that they appear immune; no action needed. If bread wheat or rye, risk is lower but still possible; proceed to step 4
4. Assess potential impact
   <<decision>>: Is severe disease development occurring (e.g., rapid lesion expansion, defoliation)?
     <<if yes>>: Expect complete defoliation, poor grain development, shrivelling, and low test weights; implement control measures (e.g., fungicide application, cultural practices) as per local recommendations
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring for progression of symptoms and environmental conditions
<<end>>

9af3097a.trigger: When assessing potential disease risks in wheat or other small grain cereals, particularly in fields with poor drainage, monocropping, or specific soil and environmental conditions.
9af3097a.content:
<<trigger>>: When assessing potential disease risks in wheat or other small grain cereals, particularly in fields with poor drainage, monocropping, or specific soil and environmental conditions.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the disease based on observed symptoms and plant parts affected.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms primarily on roots and lower stems with shiny black discoloration, and are soil temperatures cool (12-18°C) with alkaline or nutrient-deficient soils?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Take-All (Gaeumannomyces graminis f. sp. tritici). Note that nitrate enhances development; infection early in crop cycle reduces tillers and causes sterile spikes; later infections cause less damage.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Check for eye-shaped lesions on lower stem internodes with dark brown rings and straw-colored centers.
   <<decision>>: Are lesions present on lower stem internodes, with no root symptoms, and is the environment cool, damp, with high humidity at soil level?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Eyespot (Pseudocercosporella herpotrichoides). Note that wheat is most susceptible, especially winter wheat and fall-sown spring wheat; yield loss from reduced kernel size, number, and lodging.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Examine for lesions on basal leaf sheaths that are more superficial and sharply outlined than eyespot, with dark brown margins and pale centers, and mycelia easily removed by rubbing.
   <<decision>>: Are lesions superficial and sharply outlined on leaf sheaths, with possible root browning, and is the environment dry, sandy soils with cool temperatures and high humidity?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Sharp Eyespot/Rhizoctonia Root Rot (Rhizoctonia solani). Note that continuous cereal cropping, especially winter wheat, increases severity; no major epidemics reported.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Observe for darkening or browning of root, crown, and basal culm tissues, with possible white spikes before maturity or damping-off.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms general browning of roots/crown/culm, with white spikes or damping-off, and is the environment variable (warm/dry for Helminthosporium, cool/moist for Fusarium, wet for Pythium)?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Common Root Rot, Foot Rot, or Crown Rot (Helminthosporium, Fusarium, or Pythium spp.). Note that positive field identification of causal agent is difficult; localized losses from thinned stands, reduced tillers, head size, and test weights.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
5. Look for white, fluffy fungal mycelia on diseased tissues and soil, rotted culms/crowns/roots, white heads in green crop, and sclerotia on crown or soil surface.
   <<decision>>: Are there white fluffy mycelia, rotted tissues, white heads, and sclerotia present, with possible early damping-off?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Sclerotium Wilt (Southern Blight) (Corticum rolfsii). Note that early infection causes damping-off; disease leads to plant death.
     <<if no>>: No specific disease identified from this document; consult further resources.
<<end>>

130b7f7f.trigger: When a crop shows symptoms of black molds (sooty molds) such as blackened appearance of mature or dead spikes, or when wet/humid weather occurs near crop maturation, or when plants are heavily infested with aphids, or when plants die prematurely.
130b7f7f.content:
<<trigger>>: When a crop shows symptoms of black molds (sooty molds) such as blackened appearance of mature or dead spikes, or when wet/humid weather occurs near crop maturation, or when plants are heavily infested with aphids, or when plants die prematurely.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess whether the crop is at or near maturation, or if plants are heavily infested with aphids, or if plants have died prematurely.
   <<decision>>: Are wet or humid weather conditions present at or near crop maturation, or are plants heavily infested with aphids, or have plants died prematurely?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2.
     <<if no>>: No action required; black molds are not expected to develop.
2. Confirm that the affected tissue is dead or dying plant tissue (e.g., mature or dead spikes).
   <<decision>>: Is the affected tissue dead or dying?
     <<if yes>>: Recognize that black molds are saprophytic fungi (Alternaria, Cladosporium, Stemphylium, Epicoccum, and other species) and do not constitute a true disease; they invade only dead or dying tissue.
     <<if no>>: This rule does not apply; consider other pathogens.
3. Evaluate economic impact based on humidity and kernel condition.
   <<decision>>: Are humid or rainy conditions present that could allow fungi to invade mature kernels?
     <<if yes>>: Note that black molds can cause discoloration, black point, or smudge on kernels, but generally are not economically important.
     <<if no>>: Black molds are not economically important; no further action needed.
<<end>>

2c7f5dc5.trigger: When a cereal crop (wheat, barley, triticale, oats, or other grasses) shows symptoms of yellowing or reddening of leaves, stunting, upright posture of thickened stiff leaves, reduced root growth, delayed or no heading, heads that remain erect and become black and discolored during ripening, and yield reduction, and Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus (BYDV) is suspected.
2c7f5dc5.content:
<<trigger>>: When a cereal crop (wheat, barley, triticale, oats, or other grasses) shows symptoms of yellowing or reddening of leaves, stunting, upright posture of thickened stiff leaves, reduced root growth, delayed or no heading, heads that remain erect and become black and discolored during ripening, and yield reduction, and Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus (BYDV) is suspected.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess environmental conditions and infection timing
   <<decision>>: Is the temperature approximately 20°C and has it been about 14 days since potential infection?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2; conditions are favorable for BYDV development and symptom expression.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; symptoms may not yet be visible or conditions may not be optimal for disease development.
2. Evaluate aphid vector presence
   <<decision>>: Are aphid species (e.g., Rhopalosiphum padi, Schizaphis graminum, R. maidis, Metopoliphium dirhodum, Sitobion avenae, Diuraphis noxia) observed on the crop, showing symptoms such as yellowing, premature leaf death, honeydew, sooty mold, necrotic areas, purpling, leaf rolling, or white stripes?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 3; aphids may be acting as vectors for BYDV.
     <<if no>>: Consider other causes for symptoms; BYDV transmission requires aphid vectors.
3. Confirm BYDV diagnosis
   <<decision>>: Is positive identification of BYDV required using electron microscope and serological techniques?
     <<if yes>>: Use electron microscopy and serological testing to confirm the presence of BYDV.
     <<if no>>: Diagnose based on symptomology and aphid vector presence; note that symptoms may be masked or confused with other problems.
4. Assess infection timing and potential yield impact
   <<decision>>: Did infection occur early in the crop cycle?
     <<if yes>>: Expect potential yield losses of more than 20%; implement management strategies to mitigate further spread.
     <<if no>>: Yield losses may be lower; continue monitoring for disease progression.
<<end>>

1ac2d97d.trigger: When stink bugs, armyworms, cutworms, stalk borers, cereal leaf beetles, thrips, Hessian flies, or wheat stem maggots are detected or suspected in cereal crops, and the user requests a management or identification protocol.
1ac2d97d.content:
<<trigger>>: When stink bugs, armyworms, cutworms, stalk borers, cereal leaf beetles, thrips, Hessian flies, or wheat stem maggots are detected or suspected in cereal crops, and the user requests a management or identification protocol.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the pest based on symptoms and morphology.
   <<decision>>: Is the pest a shield-shaped adult insect that emits a disagreeable odor when crushed and causes kernel destruction, shriveled grain, or sterility?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as stink bug. Note that mild winters and low rainfall favor outbreaks. Proceed to step 2 for stink bug management.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 1b.
1b. <<decision>>: Is the primary symptom defoliation (chewed leaves from edges to midrib, or severed heads), with larvae feeding at night or in soil cracks, and adults are moths?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as armyworm, cutworm, or stalk borer. Note that heavy infestations can devastate large areas. Proceed to step 2 for these pests.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 1c.
1c. <<decision>>: Are there distinct longitudinal stripes on leaves, with adult beetles 4-5 mm long (black head, light brown thorax, shiny blue-green wing covers) and larvae appearing as slimy black masses due to fecal material?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as cereal leaf beetle (Oulema melanopa). Note that fall-sown cereals and wheats without hairy leaves are more affected. Proceed to step 2 for cereal leaf beetle.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 1d.
1d. <<decision>>: Are insects very small (1 mm long), brown or black, with piercing-sucking mouthparts, found behind the flag leaf sheath, causing silver coloration on tissue?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as thrips. Note that heavy rains usually destroy a high proportion of the population, and serious damage is rare. Proceed to step 2 for thrips.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 1e.
1e. <<decision>>: Is there stunting, thin stands, lodging, or broken stems, with larvae sucking sap behind leaf sheaths, and reddish-brown pupae resembling flax seeds (3-5 mm long) at nodes?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as Hessian fly (Mayetiola destructor). Note that it is one of the most destructive cereal pests, recurring annually in some regions. Proceed to step 2 for Hessian fly.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 1f.
1f. <<decision>>: Do young tillers die in fall or early spring, with infested plants showing a "white head" condition typical of stem-boring insects?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as wheat stem maggot (Meromyza americana). Proceed to step 2 for wheat stem maggot.
     <<if no>>: Pest not identified from this document. Advise user to consult additional resources.
2. Assess infestation severity and environmental factors.
   <<decision>>: For stink bugs, are conditions mild winter and low rainfall?
     <<if yes>>: Note that outbreaks are favored; monitor closely.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring as normal.
   <<decision>>: For thrips, are heavy rains occurring?
     <<if yes>>: Note that a high proportion of the population will likely be destroyed; control may not be warranted.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring.
   <<decision>>: For all pests, is the infestation level high enough to cause economic loss (e.g., yield loss of 14% to >25% for cereal leaf beetle, or severe damage for cutworms/armyworms)?
     <<if yes>>: Recommend control measures based on pest-specific thresholds (document does not specify exact thresholds or control products; advise user to consult local extension guidelines).
     <<if no>>: No action required; continue monitoring.
<<end>>

a2d07ea3.trigger: When adult flies (pale green to yellow with dark stripes, ~6 mm) are observed in wheat fields, or when symptoms of premature yellowing of the head, shriveled grain, or stem girdling are detected.
a2d07ea3.content:
<<trigger>>: When adult flies (pale green to yellow with dark stripes, ~6 mm) are observed in wheat fields, or when symptoms of premature yellowing of the head, shriveled grain, or stem girdling are detected.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the pest based on symptoms and life cycle timing.
   <<decision>>: Are the symptoms premature yellowing of the head, shriveled grain, and stem lodging with larvae girdling the stem base?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as sawfly (Cephus cinctus). Proceed to step 2 for sawfly management.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3 to assess other pests.
2. For sawfly management:
   <<decision>>: Is the wheat variety a solid or partially solid stem type?
     <<if yes>>: Note that these varieties are less susceptible; continue monitoring.
     <<if no>>: Implement control measures, especially for fall-sown cereals in the Mediterranean Basin, as sawfly can cause significant but discontinuous damage.
3. Assess for other pests if sawfly is not confirmed.
   <<decision>>: Are there patches of wilting or dying seedlings with roots severed or chewed, and are larvae (up to several cm long, with three pairs of legs) found in the soil?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as white grubs (May/June beetle larvae). Note that damage is non-uniform; if roots are not completely destroyed, plants may survive but be stunted.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Assess for wireworms.
   <<decision>>: Are seedlings wilting or dying in rows or patches, with stems chewed just above the seed, and are tough, wire-like larvae (20-30 mm, three pairs of legs) found in association with damaged seedlings?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as wireworms (click beetle larvae). Note that damage is most severe after fallow or years of grass; implement control as they are among the most damaging soil-infesting insects.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
5. Assess for slugs, snails, grasshoppers, or crickets.
   <<decision>>: Is there feeding on endosperm of germinating seed, seedlings bitten off at ground level, or longitudinal stripes chewed on leaves giving a frayed appearance (slugs/snails), or damage similar to cutworms/armyworms (grasshoppers/crickets)?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as slugs, snails, grasshoppers, or crickets. Note that distribution is localized but can cause great damage to individual stands.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 6.
6. Assess for mites.
   <<decision>>: Are there very small (<1 mm) arthropods with four pairs of legs (or two pairs for wheat curl mite), causing silvery flecking on leaves, webs, stunting, poor heading, or white discoloration?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as mites (e.g., wheat curl mite, Eriophyes tulipae). Implement control if large numbers are present.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; no specific pest identified from this document.
<<end>>

df9bdfd4.trigger: When a leaf sample shows potential mite infestation but no mites are visible to the unaided eye.
df9bdfd4.content:
<<trigger>>: When a leaf sample shows potential mite infestation but no mites are visible to the unaided eye.
<<steps>>:
1. Hold the infested leaf over a piece of white paper folded to form a trough.
   <<decision>>: Is the leaf tapped sharply several times?
     <<if yes>>: Observe whether hundreds of mites fall onto the paper and are seen moving about.
     <<if no>>: Repeat tapping until mites are dislodged or confirm absence.
<<end>>

60c7f3da.trigger: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of poor growth, discoloration, or necrosis that may be due to mineral deficiencies, toxicities, or environmental stresses.
60c7f3da.content:
<<trigger>>: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of poor growth, discoloration, or necrosis that may be due to mineral deficiencies, toxicities, or environmental stresses.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess visual symptoms to determine if the issue is likely genetic or environmental.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms consistent with genetic conditions (melanism, genetic flecking, hybrid necrosis)?
     <<if yes>>: Note that genetic flecking does not necessarily affect yield; hybrid necrosis usually appears in early generation material and affected progeny should be eliminated. No further action required unless yield is affected.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Evaluate for nutrient deficiencies based on symptom location and color.
   <<decision>>: Is the plant pale green with lower leaves yellowing from tip to sheath?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect nitrogen deficiency. Apply nitrogen fertilizer as needed.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Check for phosphorus deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are plants stunted with fewer shoots, pale to yellowish-red lower leaves, bluish-green leaf portions, purple culm bases, or small heads?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect phosphorus deficiency. Apply phosphorus fertilizer as needed.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Check for potassium deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are internodes shortened, with dry and scorched tips and margins of lower leaves?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect potassium deficiency. Apply potassium fertilizer as needed.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
5. Check for manganese deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are grayish necrotic spots or streaks on the basal portion of newest leaves, with possible kinking or twisting?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect manganese deficiency, especially in calcareous, sandy, or high organic matter soils. Apply foliar manganese sulfate.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 6.
6. Check for copper deficiency.
   <<decision>>: Are young leaf tips discolored, followed by breaking and curling, or are spikes bleached, sterile, or not emerging properly?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect copper deficiency. Apply copper fertilizer as needed.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 7.
7. Check for aluminum toxicity.
   <<decision>>: Are roots stubby and brownish, with small leaves, shortened internodes, leaf tip death, and yellow brittle old leaves?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect aluminum toxicity associated with low soil pH. Reduce toxicity by liming.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 8.
8. Check for salt stress.
   <<decision>>: Is crop growth variable within the field with barren spots, stunted dark blue-green plants, tip burn, and leaf margin firing?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect salt stress. Confirm with soil test. If excessive, manage irrigation and drainage to reduce salt buildup.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 9.
9. Check for moisture stress.
   <<decision>>: Are plants stunted with reduced tillering and root development, curling/rolling leaves during midday, reduced spikelets/florets, grain shriveling, or sterility during late booting/seed set?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect moisture stress. Ensure adequate irrigation or rainfed management.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 10.
10. Check for heat stress.
    <<decision>>: Are symptoms associated with high temperatures (increased development rate, reduced growth rate, difficult to separate from moisture stress)?
      <<if yes>>: Suspect heat stress. Manage irrigation and shading if possible.
      <<if no>>: Re-evaluate for other causes or consult further diagnostic resources.
<<end>>

99766092.trigger: When high temperatures or frost damage is suspected in wheat crops, or when herbicide phytotoxicity symptoms are observed.
99766092.content:
<<trigger>>: When high temperatures or frost damage is suspected in wheat crops, or when herbicide phytotoxicity symptoms are observed.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the type of damage based on symptoms and timing.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms leaf curling, deformed spikes, or sterility occurring near anthesis?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute damage to hormonal herbicide (e.g., 2,4-D) application too early or near anthesis; note that deformations seldom cause significant losses in small grain cereals.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Check for leaf bleaching followed by necrosis.
   <<decision>>: Are leaves bleached then necrotic, with a history of triazine (e.g., atrazine) application to the preceding crop?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute damage to triazine herbicide residues; note that damage is generally limited in small grain cereals.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Assess for frost damage symptoms.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms chlorosis, banding/striping on leaves or spikes, bleached white tissue, sterility at flowering, or separated peduncle epidermis?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute damage to frost; note that young/newly emerged tissue and flowering parts are most susceptible, and frost can be serious if late in the crop cycle.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Evaluate for high temperature damage.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms reduced spikelets, florets, or grain filling, especially during late-boot or seed-set stages, with potential for protein denaturation at very high temperatures?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute damage to high temperatures; note that flowering to maturity period often coincides with hot, dry weather, and desiccating winds with high temperatures cause major yield reductions.
     <<if no>>: Consider other causes not covered in this document.
<<end>>

1e7011f2.trigger: When leaf rust (Puccinia recondita) is suspected in wheat, triticale, or related grasses based on the presence of circular to slightly elliptical orange-brown pustules on upper leaf surfaces and sheaths.
1e7011f2.content:
<<trigger>>: When leaf rust (Puccinia recondita) is suspected in wheat, triticale, or related grasses based on the presence of circular to slightly elliptical orange-brown pustules on upper leaf surfaces and sheaths.
<<steps>>:
1. Inspect the upper surfaces of leaves and leaf sheaths for circular or slightly elliptical pustules containing orange to orange-brown urediospores, and check occasionally on the neck and awns.
   <<decision>>: Are pustules present on upper leaf surfaces or sheaths?
     <<if yes>>: Confirm identification as leaf rust; proceed to step 2.
     <<if no>>: Consider other rust diseases (e.g., stem rust with dark reddish brown pustules on stems and both leaf sides, or stripe rust) and refer to diagnostic key.
2. Assess environmental conditions for disease development risk.
   <<decision>>: Is free moisture (rain, dew) available and ambient temperature near 20°C?
     <<if yes>>: Note that disease can develop rapidly; successive urediospore generations may occur every 10-14 days; proceed to step 3.
     <<if no>>: Note that disease development is less favorable; monitor for black teliospores as plants mature or conditions change.
3. Evaluate potential yield impact based on infection timing and severity.
   <<decision>>: Are infections severe and occurring early in the growing season?
     <<if yes>>: Expect significant yield losses, primarily from reduced number of kernels per spike, test weights, and kernel quality; implement management actions (e.g., resistant varieties, fungicide application if available).
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; yield impact may be minimal.
<<end>>

2a625b8c.trigger: When monitoring wheat, barley, or triticale crops for rust or smut diseases under specific environmental conditions.
2a625b8c.content:
<<trigger>>: When monitoring wheat, barley, or triticale crops for rust or smut diseases under specific environmental conditions.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess temperature and moisture conditions to determine disease risk for stem rust (Puccinia graminis).
   <<decision>>: Are temperatures averaging about 20°C or more?
     <<if yes>>: Expect first generation of urediospores to be produced in 10-15 days; monitor for pustules and potential black teliospores as plants mature.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; moderate temperatures may delay urediospore production.
2. Assess temperature and moisture conditions to determine disease risk for stripe rust (Puccinia striiformis).
   <<decision>>: Is free moisture (rain or dew) present and temperatures between 10-20°C?
     <<if yes>>: Expect rapid disease development; monitor for yellow to orange-yellow urediospore pustules forming narrow stripes on leaves, leaf sheaths, necks, and glumes.
     <<if no>>: If temperatures exceed 25°C, expect reduced or ceased urediospore production and possible black teliospore formation; continue monitoring.
3. Evaluate for common bunt (Tilletia caries, T. foetida) or dwarf bunt (T. controversa) during seedling emergence.
   <<decision>>: Are cool temperatures present during germination and is there prolonged snow cover (for dwarf bunt)?
     <<if yes>>: Expect infection from soil-borne or seed-borne spores; monitor for bluish-green spikes, spread glumes, bunt balls replacing kernels, fetid odor, and reduced plant height (slight for common bunt, pronounced for dwarf bunt) after heading.
     <<if no>>: Infection risk is lower; continue standard monitoring.
4. Evaluate for Karnal bunt (Tilletia indica) from spike emergence through grain filling.
   <<decision>>: Are environmental conditions favorable (specific thresholds not given) during spike emergence through grain filling?
     <<if yes>>: Expect possible infection from soil-borne teliospores producing wind-borne sporidia; inspect harvested kernels for black teliospore masses replacing endosperm and fetid odor.
     <<if no>>: Disease establishment is reduced; continue monitoring.
5. Evaluate for loose smut (Ustilago tritici) during flowering.
   <<decision>>: Are cool, humid conditions present that prolong the flowering period?
     <<if yes>>: Expect wind-borne teliospores to infect developing embryos; monitor for entire inflorescence (except rachis) replaced by black spore masses, leaving bare rachis after spore dispersal.
     <<if no>>: Infection risk is lower; continue monitoring.
6. Evaluate for flag smut (Urocystis agropyri) during seedling emergence.
   <<decision>>: Are low soil moisture and cool soil temperatures present?
     <<if yes>>: Expect infection from seed- or soil-borne spores; monitor for stunted plants, profuse tillering, rolled onion-type leaves, and black subepidermal strips of teliospores on leaves, leaf sheaths, or culms near heading.
     <<if no>>: Infection risk is lower; continue monitoring.
<<end>>

8e134847.trigger: When powdery mildew (Erysiphe graminis f. sp. tritici) is detected on wheat, with white to pale gray powdery colonies on upper leaf surfaces and leaf sheaths, and environmental conditions are cool (15-22°C), cloudy, and humid (75-100% relative humidity).
8e134847.content:
<<trigger>>: When powdery mildew (Erysiphe graminis f. sp. tritici) is detected on wheat, with white to pale gray powdery colonies on upper leaf surfaces and leaf sheaths, and environmental conditions are cool (15-22°C), cloudy, and humid (75-100% relative humidity).
<<steps>>:
1. Assess infection timing and severity
   <<decision>>: Is infection occurring early in the crop cycle and conditions remain favorable for development so that high infection levels may be reached before heading?
     <<if yes>>: Initiate fungicide application to prevent major yield losses; monitor for progression to upper leaves and spikes.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; no immediate treatment required unless conditions become favorable for rapid development.
<<end>>

17e7094e.trigger: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of Fusarium Leaf Blotch (Snow Mold) at late-joint to early-boot growth stage, with oval to elliptical greyish green mottled lesions that develop into large eyespot blotches with bleached centers and leaf shredding.
17e7094e.content:
<<trigger>>: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of Fusarium Leaf Blotch (Snow Mold) at late-joint to early-boot growth stage, with oval to elliptical greyish green mottled lesions that develop into large eyespot blotches with bleached centers and leaf shredding.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess environmental conditions for disease development
   <<decision>>: Are conditions cool and moist (cool, moist weather favors development)?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2
     <<if no>>: Monitor crop; disease development is unlikely under warm, dry conditions
2. Evaluate crop type and susceptibility
   <<decision>>: Is the crop durum wheat or triticale?
     <<if yes>>: High risk; proceed to step 3
     <<if no>>: Lower risk for bread wheat or rye; oats and barley are immune; proceed to step 3 for monitoring
3. Inspect for inoculum sources (spores on crop debris left on or near soil surface)
   <<decision>>: Is crop debris present on or near the soil surface?
     <<if yes>>: Spores are likely present; proceed to step 4
     <<if no>>: Risk of infection is low; continue monitoring
4. Determine spore dispersal mechanism
   <<decision>>: Is wind or splashing rain occurring?
     <<if yes>>: Spores can be transmitted to leaves; proceed to step 5
     <<if no>>: No active dispersal; continue monitoring weather
5. Assess disease severity and potential impact
   <<decision>>: Is severe disease development observed (e.g., complete defoliation)?
     <<if yes>>: Expect poor grain development, shrivelling, and low test weights; implement management actions (e.g., fungicide application if within label timing)
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring for progression; no immediate action required
<<end>>

7a7e7328.trigger: When diagnosing potential root and stem diseases in wheat or other small grain cereals in temperate regions, based on observed symptoms and field conditions.
7a7e7328.content:
<<trigger>>: When diagnosing potential root and stem diseases in wheat or other small grain cereals in temperate regions, based on observed symptoms and field conditions.
<<steps>>:
1. Observe symptoms on roots, lower stems, and leaf sheaths.
   <<decision>>: Are roots and lower stems shiny black, with stunted plants and whitened stems/spikes?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2 (Take-All assessment).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
2. Assess for Take-All (Gaeumannomyces graminis f. sp. tritici).
   <<decision>>: Are soil temperatures cool (12-18°C), soils alkaline or nutrient deficient, or is nitrate fertilizer used?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Take-All. Note that infection is favored by cool soil temperatures (12-18°C), alkaline or nutrient deficient soils, and nitrate. Early infection reduces tillers and causes sterile spikes; later infection is less damaging.
     <<if no>>: Consider other diseases; Take-All is less likely.
3. Observe for eye-shaped lesions on lower stem internodes.
   <<decision>>: Are there elliptical lesions with dark brown to greenish brown rings and straw-colored centers on lower stem internodes, potentially causing stem breakage near ground?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 4 (Eyespot assessment).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
4. Assess for Eyespot (Pseudocercosporella herpotrichoides).
   <<decision>>: Is the weather cool and damp, with high humidity at soil level, and is the crop fall-sown wheat?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Eyespot. Note that symptoms do not appear on roots; disease can kill tillers or whole plants, and yield loss results from reduced kernel size/number and lodging.
     <<if no>>: Consider other diseases; Eyespot is less likely.
5. Observe for lesions on basal leaf sheaths similar to eyespot but more superficial and sharply outlined.
   <<decision>>: Are lesions superficial with dark brown margins and pale straw-colored centers, with easily removable mycelia, and are roots brown and reduced in number?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 6 (Sharp Eyespot/Rhizoctonia Root Rot assessment).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 7.
6. Assess for Sharp Eyespot and Rhizoctonia Root Rot (Rhizoctonia solani).
   <<decision>>: Are soils dry and sandy, with cool temperatures and high humidity, and is the field continuously sown to cereals (especially winter wheat)?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Sharp Eyespot/Rhizoctonia Root Rot. Note that disease can cause stunting and reduced tillers; no major epidemics reported.
     <<if no>>: Consider other diseases; Rhizoctonia is less likely.
7. Observe for darkening or browning of root, crown, and basal culm tissues, with possible white spikes before maturity.
   <<decision>>: Are there darkened/browned roots, crown, or basal culm tissues, with possible lodging or white spikes, and possible pre- or post-emergence damping off?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 8 (Common Root Rot, Foot Rot, Crown Rot assessment).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 9.
8. Assess for Common Root Rot, Foot Rot, and Crown Rot (Helminthosporium, Fusarium, Pythium spp.).
   <<decision>>: Are soils warm and dry with plants under stress?
     <<if yes>>: Likely Helminthosporium spp. (common root rot).
     <<if no>>: Are soils cool and moist?
       <<if yes>>: Likely Fusarium spp. (root, foot, and crown rots).
       <<if no>>: Are soils wet?
         <<if yes>>: Likely Pythium spp.
         <<if no>>: Positive field identification is difficult; consider lab analysis.
9. Observe for white, fluffy fungal mycelia on tissues and soil, with rotted culms, crowns, roots, and sclerotia near soil surface.
   <<decision>>: Are there white, fluffy mycelia on diseased tissues and surrounding soil, with rotted culms/crowns/roots, white heads/spikes, and sclerotia present?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 10 (Sclerotium Wilt assessment).
     <<if no>>: Re-evaluate symptoms; disease may not match described conditions.
10. Assess for Sclerotium Wilt (Southern Blight) (Corticum rolfsii).
    <<decision>>: Did infection occur early in the crop cycle, causing pre- or post-emergence damping off?
      <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Sclerotium Wilt. Note that disease leads to plant death and white heads/spikes.
      <<if no>>: Consider later-stage infection; still possible but less typical.
<<end>>

5dd3d962.trigger: When a crop shows symptoms of black molds (sooty molds) such as blackened appearance of mature or dead spikes, or when wet/humid weather occurs near crop maturation, or when plants are heavily infested with aphids, or when plants die prematurely.
5dd3d962.content:
<<trigger>>: When a crop shows symptoms of black molds (sooty molds) such as blackened appearance of mature or dead spikes, or when wet/humid weather occurs near crop maturation, or when plants are heavily infested with aphids, or when plants die prematurely.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess whether the crop is at or near maturation, or if plants are heavily infested with aphids, or if plants have died prematurely.
   <<decision>>: Are wet or humid weather conditions present at or near crop maturation, or are plants heavily infested with aphids, or have plants died prematurely?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2.
     <<if no>>: No action required; black molds are not expected to develop.
2. Confirm that the affected tissue is dead or dying plant tissue (e.g., mature or dead spikes).
   <<decision>>: Is the affected tissue dead or dying?
     <<if yes>>: Recognize that black molds are saprophytic fungi (Alternaria, Cladosporium, Stemphylium, Epicoccum, and other species) and do not constitute a true disease; they invade only dead or dying tissue.
     <<if no>>: The symptoms are not caused by black molds; investigate other pathogens or disorders.
3. Evaluate economic impact based on humidity and kernel condition.
   <<decision>>: Are humid or rainy conditions present that could allow fungi to invade mature kernels?
     <<if yes>>: Note that black molds may cause discoloration, black point, or smudge on kernels, but generally are not economically important.
     <<if no>>: Black molds are not economically important; no further action needed.
<<end>>

96bbba3a.trigger: When a cereal crop (wheat, barley, triticale, oats, or other grasses) shows symptoms of yellowing or reddening of leaves, stunting, upright posture of thickened stiff leaves, reduced root growth, delayed or no heading, yield reduction, or heads that remain erect and become black and discolored during ripening, and Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus (BYDV) is suspected.
96bbba3a.content:
<<trigger>>: When a cereal crop (wheat, barley, triticale, oats, or other grasses) shows symptoms of yellowing or reddening of leaves, stunting, upright posture of thickened stiff leaves, reduced root growth, delayed or no heading, yield reduction, or heads that remain erect and become black and discolored during ripening, and Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus (BYDV) is suspected.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess environmental conditions and timing
   <<decision>>: Is the temperature approximately 20°C and have symptoms appeared approximately 14 days after potential infection?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2.
     <<if no>>: Consider other causes, as these conditions are favorable for BYDV development.
2. Identify potential aphid vectors in the field
   <<decision>>: Are aphids present, specifically species such as Rhopalosiphum padi, Schizaphis graminum, R. maidis, Metopoliphium dirhodum, Sitobion avenae, or Diuraphis noxia?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 3.
     <<if no>>: Consider other causes, as BYDV is aphid-transmitted.
3. Evaluate infection timing and potential yield impact
   <<decision>>: Did the infection occur early in the crop cycle?
     <<if yes>>: Expect yield losses of more than 20%, and potentially much larger losses.
     <<if no>>: Yield loss may be lower, but monitor crop development.
4. Confirm diagnosis using specialized techniques
   <<decision>>: Is positive identification required beyond visual symptoms?
     <<if yes>>: Use an electron microscope and serological techniques for confirmation.
     <<if no>>: Rely on symptom observation and vector presence for preliminary diagnosis.
<<end>>

7a84756f.trigger: When stink bugs, armyworms, cutworms, stalk borers, cereal leaf beetles, thrips, Hessian flies, or wheat stem maggots are detected or suspected in cereal crops, and the user requests a diagnostic or management response based on the document.
7a84756f.content:
<<trigger>>: When stink bugs, armyworms, cutworms, stalk borers, cereal leaf beetles, thrips, Hessian flies, or wheat stem maggots are detected or suspected in cereal crops, and the user requests a diagnostic or management response based on the document.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the pest based on symptoms and morphology described in the document.
   <<decision>>: Is the pest a shield-shaped adult insect that emits a disagreeable odor when crushed, and is feeding on developing heads or kernels?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as stink bug. Note that feeding during early development destroys the kernel, later feeding shrivels grain, and may cause partial or total sterility. Overwinters as adults under dead leaves/grass; migrates to cereals in spring. Mild winters and low rainfall favor outbreaks.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Check for defoliation or stem/head severing symptoms.
   <<decision>>: Is the primary symptom defoliation (larvae chewing leaves from edges to midrib) or larvae severing the neck below the head, with larvae found in soil cracks or under rocks during day, feeding at night or early morning?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as armyworms, cutworms, or stalk borers. Note that larvae are omnivorous on grasses; adults are moths laying eggs on leaves near ground. Heavy infestations can devastate large areas.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Check for longitudinal stripes on leaves and presence of small (4-5 mm) beetles with black head, light brown thorax, shiny blue-green wing covers, or slimy yellow larvae with fecal mass on back.
   <<decision>>: Are these symptoms present, and is the crop fall-sown wheat (especially with non-hairy leaves)?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as cereal leaf beetle (Oulema melanopa). Note one generation per year; adults overwinter under plant debris. Yield losses of 14% to >25% possible in winter wheat and fall-sown spring wheat.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Check for small (1 mm) brown or black insects with piercing-sucking mouthparts, found behind flag leaf sheath, causing silver coloration on tissue.
   <<decision>>: Are these symptoms present, and are large numbers causing silver tissue?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as thrips. Note very short generation time (10+ generations/year); heavy rains destroy high proportion of population. Rarely cause serious damage warranting control.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
5. Check for stunting, thin stands, lodging, or stems breaking prior to maturity, with small (3-4 mm) flies having black head/thorax and pinkish/yellow-brown abdomen, and reddish-brown pupae ("flag seed") behind leaf sheaths at nodes.
   <<decision>>: Are these symptoms present, and is the crop wheat (or barley, rye)?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as Hessian fly (Mayetiola destructor). Note larvae suck sap; adults emerge in spring from overwintered pupae in straw/stubble; eggs laid in rows on upper leaf sides. One of the most destructive cereal pests; recurs annually in some regions (e.g., North Africa, USA).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 6.
6. Check for "white head" condition and death of young tillers in fall or early spring.
   <<decision>>: Are these symptoms present?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as wheat stem maggot (Meromyza americana). Note that attacked tillers usually die.
     <<if no>>: No specific pest identified from document; advise further investigation.
<<end>>

8bf2f0c1.trigger: When adult flies (pale green to yellow with dark stripes, ~6 mm) are observed in wheat fields, or when symptoms of stem girdling, premature yellowing of the head, shriveled grain, or lodging are detected.
8bf2f0c1.content:
<<trigger>>: When adult flies (pale green to yellow with dark stripes, ~6 mm) are observed in wheat fields, or when symptoms of stem girdling, premature yellowing of the head, shriveled grain, or lodging are detected.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the pest based on symptoms and life cycle timing.
   <<decision>>: Are the symptoms premature yellowing of the head, shriveled grain, stem girdling, and lodging, with adults appearing from late spring to midsummer?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed with sawfly (Cephus cinctus) management: note that fall-sown cereals are more commonly attacked and wheat lines with solid or partially solid stems are less susceptible; monitor for discontinuous infestations.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Assess if damage includes wilting or dying patches of seedlings with roots severed or chewed.
   <<decision>>: Are there patches of wilting/dying plants (especially at seedling stage) with roots partially or completely severed, and are large larvae (up to several cm long, ~1 cm thick, with three pairs of legs) found in the soil?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as white grubs (May/June beetle larvae). Note that damage may be severe if seeded into heavily infested grasslands; plants may survive if roots not completely destroyed but will be stunted and fail to produce heads.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Check for wireworm damage: wilting/dying adjacent plants in a row or patch, stems chewed just above the seed, and seed endosperm eaten leaving only seed coat.
   <<decision>>: Are there wilting/dying adjacent plants with stems chewed just above the seed, and are tough, wire-like larvae (20-30 mm, three pairs of legs, cream to brown) found in association with damaged seedlings?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as wireworms (click beetle larvae). Note that damage is most severe where wheat is seeded after fallow or after several years of grass; generations overlap so all sizes may be present.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Examine for damage from slugs, snails, grasshoppers, or crickets.
   <<decision>>: Is there feeding on endosperm of germinating seed, seedlings bitten off at ground level, or longitudinal stripes chewed on leaves (frayed appearance) from slugs/snails, OR damage similar to cutworms/armyworms from grasshoppers/crickets?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as slugs, snails, grasshoppers, or crickets. Note that these pests are usually localized but can cause great damage to individual wheat stands.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
5. Inspect for mite infestation: look for silvery flecking on leaves, webs, stunted plants, poor heading, or white discoloration.
   <<decision>>: Are mites (adults <1 mm, usually four pairs of legs, but wheat curl mite has two pairs) present in large numbers causing silvery flecking, stunting, poor heading, or white plants?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as mite infestation. Note that mites are not insects; individual mites are barely visible.
     <<if no>>: Re-evaluate field for other causes or consult further agronomic guidance.
<<end>>

2007e6f8.trigger: When a cereal crop shows symptoms of stunting, chlorosis, root knots, or galls, and nematode infestation is suspected based on field observations.
2007e6f8.content:
<<trigger>>: When a cereal crop shows symptoms of stunting, chlorosis, root knots, or galls, and nematode infestation is suspected based on field observations.
<<steps>>:
1. Collect plant samples (roots, leaves, or seed heads) and soil from affected areas.
   <<decision>>: Are seed galls present in florets, replacing kernels with dark brown, seed-shaped structures?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as Seed Gall Nematode (Anguina tritici); note that it is rarely of economic importance and can vector Corynebacterium tritici.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Examine roots of seedlings for frequent branching, swellings, or cysts.
   <<decision>>: Are off-white to dark brown cysts present on roots, with root branching and swelling?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as Cereal Cyst Nematode (Heterodera avenae); note that significant yield losses can occur when populations are high, and all wheat cultivars are susceptible but some do not support cyst formation.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Inspect root tips for small knots or galls, and check for stunting and chlorosis above ground.
   <<decision>>: Are small knots or galls present near root tips, with possible excessive root branching?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as Root Knot Nematode (Meloidogyne spp.); note that damage depends on number of egg masses in soil, all winter and spring wheat cultivars are compatible hosts, and seedlings may be killed in extreme attacks.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Assess for physiological or genetic disorders if no pathogen is identified.
   <<decision>>: Are leaf spots, blotches, or chlorosis present without identifiable pathogen, especially after heading or following cool, cloudy weather then hot, sunny conditions?
     <<if yes>>: Consider physiological leaf spot (e.g., manganese deficiency or "splotch"); note that it is usually not serious and breeding efforts eliminate prone genotypes.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
5. Check for brownish black to dark purple spots on leaf sheaths, stems, or glumes.
   <<decision>>: Are melanoid pigmentation spots present on glumes and peduncles, especially under cloudy, humid weather with high ultraviolet light?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as Melanism and Brown Necrosis (False Black Chaff); note that it may be confused with bacterial black chaff or septoria glume blotch.
     <<if no>>: Conclude that the disorder may be due to other physiologic, genetic, or environmental factors not specified in the document.
<<end>>

8596eae2.trigger: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of poor growth, discoloration, or necrosis that may be due to mineral deficiencies, toxicities, or environmental stresses.
8596eae2.content:
<<trigger>>: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of poor growth, discoloration, or necrosis that may be due to mineral deficiencies, toxicities, or environmental stresses.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess visual symptoms and field conditions to determine the likely cause.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms pale green lower leaves with yellowing from tip to sheath, possibly followed by necrosis?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as nitrogen deficiency; apply nitrogen fertilizer as per standard agronomic rates.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Check for stunted plants with fewer shoots, pale to yellowish red leaves starting from lower leaves, bluish-green leaf portions, purple culm bases, and small heads.
   <<decision>>: Are these symptoms present?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as phosphorus deficiency; apply phosphorus fertilizer as per standard agronomic rates.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Check for shortened internodes, dry and scorched tips and margins of lower leaves.
   <<decision>>: Are these symptoms present?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as potassium deficiency; apply potassium fertilizer as per standard agronomic rates.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Check for grayish necrotic spots or streaks on the basal portion of the newest leaves, possibly causing kinking or twisting.
   <<decision>>: Are these symptoms present?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as manganese deficiency; apply foliar manganese sulfate to alleviate deficiency.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
5. Check for discoloration of young leaf tips, followed by breaking and curling of leaves, bleached and sterile spikes, or poor spike emergence.
   <<decision>>: Are these symptoms present?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as copper deficiency; apply copper fertilizer as per standard agronomic rates.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 6.
6. Check for stubby, brownish roots, small leaves, shortened and thickened internodes, dying leaf tips, and yellow brittle old leaves.
   <<decision>>: Are these symptoms present and is soil pH low?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as aluminum toxicity; reduce toxicity by liming the soil.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 7.
7. Check for variable crop growth within the field (barren spots), stunted dark blue-green plants with tip burn and firing on leaf margins.
   <<decision>>: Are these symptoms present?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as salt stress; confirm with a soil test for excessive salt levels.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 8.
8. Check for stunted plants, reduced tillering and root development, curling and rolling of leaves during midday, reduced spikelets/florets, grain shrivelling, or sterility during late booting/seed set.
   <<decision>>: Are these symptoms present?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as moisture stress; manage irrigation or rainfed practices accordingly.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 9.
9. Check for symptoms associated with high temperatures (often combined with moisture stress), such as increased development rate and reduced growth rate.
   <<decision>>: Are these symptoms present?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as heat stress; manage irrigation and shading if possible.
     <<if no>>: Consider genetic causes (genetic flecking, hybrid necrosis, melanism) as non-serious or requiring elimination of affected progeny in early generation material.
<<end>>

19671344.trigger: When high temperatures or frost damage is suspected in wheat crops, or when herbicide phytotoxicity from 2,4-D or triazine residues is observed.
19671344.content:
<<trigger>>: When high temperatures or frost damage is suspected in wheat crops, or when herbicide phytotoxicity from 2,4-D or triazine residues is observed.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the type of damage based on symptoms and timing.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms leaf curling and deformed spikes, or sterility near anthesis?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute damage to 2,4-D herbicide applied too early or near anthesis; note that deformations seldom cause significant losses in small grain cereals.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Assess for triazine herbicide residue damage.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms leaf bleaching followed by necrosis, with a history of triazine (e.g., atrazine) application to the preceding crop?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute damage to triazine residues; note that damage results from excessive amounts, wrong growth stage, or wrong species.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Assess for frost damage.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms chlorosis, banding/striping on leaves or spikes, bleached white tissue, sterility at flowering, or separated peduncle epidermis?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute damage to frost; note that young or newly emerged tissue and flowering parts are most susceptible, and frost can be serious if late in the crop cycle.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Assess for high temperature damage.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms reduced spikelets, florets, or grain filling, especially during late-boot or seed-set stages, possibly with desiccating winds?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute damage to high temperatures; note that very high temperatures can kill plants by denaturing proteins, and flowering to maturity period in wheat often coincides with hot, dry weather.
     <<if no>>: Conclude that damage is not clearly attributable to the described causes; consider other factors.
<<end>>

06902428.trigger: When leaf rust (brown rust) caused by Puccinia recondita is suspected in wheat, triticale, or related grasses based on field symptoms of circular to slightly elliptical orange to orange-brown pustules on upper leaf surfaces and leaf sheaths.
06902428.content:
<<trigger>>: When leaf rust (brown rust) caused by Puccinia recondita is suspected in wheat, triticale, or related grasses based on field symptoms of circular to slightly elliptical orange to orange-brown pustules on upper leaf surfaces and leaf sheaths.
<<steps>>:
1. Confirm presence of leaf rust by examining plants for circular or slightly elliptical pustules, smaller than stem rust pustules, containing orange to orange-brown urediospores, primarily on upper surfaces of leaves and leaf sheaths, and occasionally on the neck and awns.
   <<decision>>: Are pustules dark reddish brown, occurring on both sides of leaves, stems, and spikes, with a ragged and torn appearance?
     <<if yes>>: This indicates stem rust (Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici), not leaf rust. Follow stem rust management protocol.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Assess environmental conditions for disease development.
   <<decision>>: Is free moisture (rain or dew) available and ambient temperature near 20°C?
     <<if yes>>: Disease can develop rapidly. Proceed to step 3.
     <<if no>>: Disease development is less favorable. Monitor conditions and re-evaluate when free moisture and temperatures near 20°C occur.
3. Evaluate disease severity and potential yield impact.
   <<decision>>: Are infections severe and occurring early in the growing season?
     <<if yes>>: Significant yield losses may occur, primarily by reducing number of kernels per spike, test weights, and kernel quality. Implement control measures.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; successive generations of urediospores can be produced every 10-14 days if conditions remain favorable.
4. Monitor for signs of plant maturity or unfavorable environmental conditions.
   <<decision>>: Are masses of black teliospores becoming evident on plants?
     <<if yes>>: This indicates the disease is transitioning to the overwintering stage; further spread of urediospores is unlikely.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring for continued urediospore production and potential spread.
<<end>>

6421963a.trigger: When monitoring wheat, barley, or triticale crops for rust diseases (stem rust or stripe rust) and environmental conditions are favorable for disease development.
6421963a.content:
<<trigger>>: When monitoring wheat, barley, or triticale crops for rust diseases (stem rust or stripe rust) and environmental conditions are favorable for disease development.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess average temperature and moisture conditions for stem rust risk
   <<decision>>: Is the average temperature about 20°C or more?
     <<if yes>>: Expect first generation of urediospores to be produced in 10-15 days; monitor for pustules containing reddish-brown urediospores on stems and leaf sheaths.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring; moderate temperatures may still allow slower development.
2. Assess temperature and moisture conditions for stripe rust risk
   <<decision>>: Is free moisture (rain or dew) present and temperature between 10-20°C?
     <<if yes>>: Expect rapid disease development; monitor for yellow to orange-yellow urediospores forming narrow stripes on leaves, leaf sheaths, necks, and glumes.
     <<if no>>: If temperature is above 25°C, note that urediospore production is reduced or ceases and black teliospores may be produced; continue monitoring.
3. Evaluate crop stage and infection timing for stem rust severity
   <<decision>>: Did infection occur during early crop stages?
     <<if yes>>: Anticipate severe effects including reductions in tillering and losses in grain weight and quality; under favorable conditions, complete crop loss can occur.
     <<if no>>: Effects may be less severe; continue standard monitoring.
4. Monitor for black teliospore production as plants mature
   <<decision>>: Are masses of black teliospores observed on stems or leaves?
     <<if yes>>: Note that this indicates late-stage disease progression; assess overall crop impact.
     <<if no>>: Continue regular scouting for pustules and stripes.
<<end>>

942d9491.trigger: When powdery mildew (Erysiphe graminis f. sp. tritici) is detected on wheat, with symptoms of white to pale gray powdery colonies on upper leaf surfaces and leaf sheaths, and environmental conditions are cool (15-22°C), cloudy, and humid (75-100% relative humidity).
942d9491.content:
<<trigger>>: When powdery mildew (Erysiphe graminis f. sp. tritici) is detected on wheat, with symptoms of white to pale gray powdery colonies on upper leaf surfaces and leaf sheaths, and environmental conditions are cool (15-22°C), cloudy, and humid (75-100% relative humidity).
<<steps>>:
1. Assess infection timing and severity
   <<decision>>: Is infection occurring early in the crop cycle and are conditions remaining favorable for development so that high infection levels are reached before heading?
     <<if yes>>: Initiate fungicide application to prevent major yield losses (specific product and dosage not specified in document; consult local recommendations).
     <<if no>>: Monitor crop; no immediate action required unless conditions become favorable for further development.
<<end>>

cd75b5dc.trigger: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of Fusarium Leaf Blotch (Snow Mold) at late-joint to early-boot growth stage, with oval to elliptical greyish green mottled lesions that develop into large eyespot blotches with bleached centers and leaf shredding.
cd75b5dc.content:
<<trigger>>: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of Fusarium Leaf Blotch (Snow Mold) at late-joint to early-boot growth stage, with oval to elliptical greyish green mottled lesions that develop into large eyespot blotches with bleached centers and leaf shredding.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess environmental conditions for disease development
   <<decision>>: Are conditions cool and moist (cool, moist weather)?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2
     <<if no>>: Monitor crop; disease development is not favored under current conditions
2. Evaluate crop type and susceptibility
   <<decision>>: Is the crop durum wheat or triticale?
     <<if yes>>: High risk; proceed to step 3
     <<if no>>: Lower risk for bread wheat or rye; oats and barley are immune; monitor as needed
3. Check for presence of crop debris on or near soil surface
   <<decision>>: Is crop debris present on or near the soil surface?
     <<if yes>>: Spores are likely produced on debris; proceed to step 4
     <<if no>>: Risk of spore transmission is reduced; continue monitoring
4. Determine if spores can be transmitted to leaves
   <<decision>>: Is there wind or splashing rain to transmit spores from debris to leaves?
     <<if yes>>: Infection is likely; proceed to step 5
     <<if no>>: Transmission is unlikely; monitor weather for changes
5. Assess potential for severe disease development
   <<decision>>: Could severe disease development cause complete defoliation?
     <<if yes>>: Expect poor grain development, shriveling, and low test weights; implement management actions (e.g., fungicide application if available and permitted)
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring for progression
<<end>>

d0df06c6.trigger: When diagnosing potential root and stem diseases in wheat or other small grain cereals in temperate regions, based on observed symptoms and field conditions.
d0df06c6.content:
<<trigger>>: When diagnosing potential root and stem diseases in wheat or other small grain cereals in temperate regions, based on observed symptoms and field conditions.
<<steps>>:
1. Observe symptoms on roots, stems, and leaf sheaths.
   <<decision>>: Are roots and lower stems shiny black, with stunted plants and whitened stems/spikes?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2 for Take-All (Gaeumannomyces graminis).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
2. Assess Take-All risk factors.
   <<decision>>: Are soil temperatures cool (12-18°C), soils alkaline or nutrient deficient, and nitrate present, with infection occurring in fall or early spring?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Take-All; note that early infection reduces tillers and causes sterile spikes, and disease is widespread in monocropped areas with liming or minimum tillage.
     <<if no>>: Consider later-season infection causing less damage, confined to roots.
3. Observe for eye-shaped lesions on lower stem internodes.
   <<decision>>: Are there elliptical lesions with dark brown to greenish brown rings and straw-colored centers on the lower stem, without root symptoms?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 4 for Eyespot (Pseudocercosporella herpotrichoides).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
4. Assess Eyespot risk factors.
   <<decision>>: Are conditions cool, damp, with high humidity at soil level, and is the crop fall-sown wheat?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Eyespot; expect potential lodging, reduced kernel size/number, and tiller death.
     <<if no>>: Consider other diseases.
5. Observe for lesions similar to eyespot but more superficial and sharply outlined, with easily removable mycelia.
   <<decision>>: Are lesions on basal leaf sheaths with dark brown margins and pale centers, and are roots brown and reduced in number?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 6 for Sharp Eyespot/Rhizoctonia Root Rot (Rhizoctonia solani).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 7.
6. Assess Sharp Eyespot risk factors.
   <<decision>>: Are soils dry, sandy, with cool temperatures and high humidity, and is the field continuously sown to cereals (especially winter wheat)?
     <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Sharp Eyespot; note stunting and reduced tillers, but no major epidemics reported.
     <<if no>>: Consider other pathogens.
7. Observe for darkening or browning of root, crown, and basal culm tissues, with white spikes before maturity.
   <<decision>>: Are there signs of pre- or post-emergence damping off, or lodging?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 8 for Common Root Rot, Foot Rot, or Crown Rot (Helminthosporium, Fusarium, Pythium spp.).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 9.
8. Assess Common Root Rot complex risk factors.
   <<decision>>: Are soils warm and dry with plants under stress?
     <<if yes>>: Likely Helminthosporium spp. (common root rot).
     <<if no>>: Are soils cool and moist?
       <<if yes>>: Likely Fusarium spp. (foot/crown rot).
       <<if no>>: Are soils wet?
         <<if yes>>: Likely Pythium spp.
         <<if no>>: Diagnosis uncertain; note positive field identification is difficult.
9. Observe for white, fluffy mycelia on tissues and soil, with sclerotia on crown or near soil surface.
   <<decision>>: Are there rotted culms, crowns, roots, and white heads/spikes in green crop, with sclerotia present?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 10 for Sclerotium Wilt (Corticum rolfsii).
     <<if no>>: Re-evaluate symptoms or consider other diseases not covered.
10. Assess Sclerotium Wilt risk factors.
    <<decision>>: Did infection occur early in the crop cycle, causing damping off?
      <<if yes>>: Diagnose as Sclerotium Wilt; expect plant death and white heads.
      <<if no>>: Consider later-stage infection.
<<end>>

21a0426f.trigger: When a crop shows symptoms of black molds (sooty molds) such as blackened appearance of mature or dead spikes, or when wet/humid weather occurs near crop maturation, or when plants are heavily infested with aphids, or when plants die prematurely.
21a0426f.content:
<<trigger>>: When a crop shows symptoms of black molds (sooty molds) such as blackened appearance of mature or dead spikes, or when wet/humid weather occurs near crop maturation, or when plants are heavily infested with aphids, or when plants die prematurely.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess whether the crop is at or near maturation, or if plants are heavily infested with aphids, or if plants have died prematurely.
   <<decision>>: Are wet or humid weather conditions present at or near crop maturation, or are plants heavily infested with aphids, or have plants died prematurely?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2.
     <<if no>>: No action required; black molds are not expected to develop.
2. Confirm that the affected tissue is dead or dying, as black molds are saprophytic and only invade such tissue.
   <<decision>>: Is the affected plant tissue dead or dying?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 3.
     <<if no>>: This is not black mold; investigate other potential diseases or disorders.
3. Evaluate economic impact by checking if humid or rainy conditions are present and if mature kernels are affected.
