   <<decision>>: Are humid or rainy conditions present, and are mature kernels being invaded, causing discoloration, black point, or smudge?
     <<if yes>>: Note that black molds can cause kernel discoloration, black point, or smudge, but generally are not economically important; monitor for quality impacts.
     <<if no>>: No significant economic impact expected; black molds are generally not economically important.
<<end>>

63c40f45.trigger: When a cereal crop (wheat, barley, triticale, oats, or other grasses) shows symptoms of yellowing or reddening of leaves, stunting, upright thickened stiff leaves, reduced root growth, delayed or no heading, heads that remain erect and become black and discolored during ripening, and yield reduction, and Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus (BYDV) is suspected.
63c40f45.content:
<<trigger>>: When a cereal crop (wheat, barley, triticale, oats, or other grasses) shows symptoms of yellowing or reddening of leaves, stunting, upright thickened stiff leaves, reduced root growth, delayed or no heading, heads that remain erect and become black and discolored during ripening, and yield reduction, and Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus (BYDV) is suspected.
<<steps>>:
1. Confirm disease presence by observing symptoms and considering environmental conditions.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms consistent with BYDV (yellowing or reddening of leaves, stunting, upright thickened stiff leaves, reduced root growth, delayed or no heading, black discolored heads during ripening) and is the temperature approximately 20°C?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2.
     <<if no>>: Consider other causes (e.g., other diseases, insect pests, nutrient deficiencies) and consult diagnostic guide for alternative symptoms.
2. Assess timing of infection relative to crop cycle.
   <<decision>>: Did infection occur early in the crop cycle?
     <<if yes>>: Expect potential yield losses of more than 20%; prioritize management actions.
     <<if no>>: Expect lower yield impact; continue monitoring.
3. Identify and monitor aphid vectors (e.g., Rhopalosiphum padi, Schizaphis graminum, R. maidis, Metopoliphium dirhodum, Sitobion avenae, Diuraphis noxia) in the field.
   <<decision>>: Are aphids present in sufficient numbers to cause damage or act as vectors?
     <<if yes>>: Implement aphid control measures to reduce virus spread; note that aphid feeding can cause yellowing, premature leaf death, honeydew, sooty molds, necrotic areas, purpling, leaf rolling, or white stripes.
     <<if no>>: Continue monitoring for aphid presence and disease progression.
4. Evaluate disease development timeline.
   <<decision>>: Have approximately 14 days passed since infection under favorable temperatures (~20°C)?
     <<if yes>>: Symptoms are expected to appear; confirm diagnosis and assess severity.
     <<if no>>: Continue observation; symptoms may still develop.
<<end>>

00677c17.trigger: When stink bugs, armyworms, cutworms, stalk borers, cereal leaf beetles, thrips, Hessian flies, or wheat stem maggots are detected or suspected in cereal crops.
00677c17.content:
<<trigger>>: When stink bugs, armyworms, cutworms, stalk borers, cereal leaf beetles, thrips, Hessian flies, or wheat stem maggots are detected or suspected in cereal crops.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the pest species based on symptoms and morphology
   <<decision>>: Is the pest a shield-shaped adult bug that emits a disagreeable odor when crushed?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as stink bug. Note that feeding on developing heads may cause partial or total sterility; feeding during later stages shrivels grain; mild winters and low rainfall favor outbreaks.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 1b
   <<decision>>: Is the primary symptom defoliation, with larvae chewing leaves from edges to midrib or severing the neck below the head?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as armyworm, cutworm, or stalk borer. Note larvae may feed at soil surface, underground on roots, or inside stems; they feed at night or early morning, or all day in damp weather.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 1c
   <<decision>>: Are there distinct longitudinal stripes on leaves, with adult beetles 4-5 mm long (black head, light brown thorax, shiny blue-green wing covers) and larvae appearing as slimy black masses?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as cereal leaf beetle (Oulema melanopa). Note it produces one generation per year; adults overwinter under plant debris; hairy-leaved wheats are less affected.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 1d
   <<decision>>: Are insects very small (1 mm long), brown or black, with piercing-sucking mouthparts, found behind flag leaf sheath, causing silver coloration on tissue?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as thrips. Note generation time is very short (10+ generations per year); heavy rains destroy high proportion of population; rarely cause serious damage warranting control.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 1e
   <<decision>>: Are plants stunted with thin stands, lodging, and reduced yield; larvae sucking juices; reddish brown pupae ("flag seed") found behind leaf sheaths at nodes; adult flies 3-4 mm with black head/thorax and pinkish/yellow-brown abdomen?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as Hessian fly (Mayetiola destructor). Note eggs laid in rows on upper leaf sides; larvae settle behind leaf sheaths; pupae overwinter in straw or stubble; mainly pest of wheat but may attack barley, rye, grasses.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 1f
   <<decision>>: Do young tillers die when attacked in fall or early spring, with infested plants showing "white head" condition?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as wheat stem maggot (Meromyza americana).
     <<if no>>: Consult additional identification resources (not covered in document).

2. Assess infestation severity and risk factors
   <<decision>>: For stink bugs, have there been mild winters and low rainfall?
     <<if yes>>: Note that outbreaks are favored; losses depend on insect density, weather, and crop duration; losses primarily reduce baking quality.
     <<if no>>: Note that outbreaks are less favored.
   <<decision>>: For armyworms/cutworms/stalk borers, is infestation heavy?
     <<if yes>>: Note that they can be very destructive and devastate large areas; larvae may sever neck below head.
     <<if no>>: Note that damage is sporadic.
   <<decision>>: For cereal leaf beetle, is the crop fall-sown wheat (especially winter wheat or fall-sown spring wheat)?
     <<if yes>>: Note that significant yield losses of 14% to over 25% can occur; hairy-leaved wheats are less affected.
     <<if no>>: Note that risk is lower.
   <<decision>>: For thrips, are numbers large enough to cause silver coloration?
     <<if yes>>: Note that damage may occur, but it is unusual to find infestations warranting control.
     <<if no>>: Note that thrips rarely cause serious damage.
   <<decision>>: For Hessian fly, is the crop wheat or other cereals (barley, rye, grasses)?
     <<if yes>>: Note that this is one of the most destructive insect pests; widespread outbreaks occur; in North Africa and USA, pest recurs annually.
     <<if no>>: Note that risk is lower.
   <<decision>>: For wheat stem maggot, are young tillers attacked in fall or early spring?
     <<if yes>>: Note that tillers usually die, producing "white head" condition.
     <<if no>>: Note that damage may be less severe.

3. Determine control action based on pest and severity
   <<decision>>: Is the pest thrips?
     <<if yes>>: No control action is typically warranted as infestations rarely reach damaging levels.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3b
   <<decision>>: Is the pest cereal leaf beetle on winter wheat or fall-sown spring wheat with significant infestation?
     <<if yes>>: Implement control measures to prevent yield losses of 14-25% or more.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3c
   <<decision>>: Is the pest Hessian fly in a wheat-growing area with history of recurrence (e.g., North Africa, USA)?
     <<if yes>>: Implement control measures as this is one of the most destructive pests; monitor for stunting, thin stands, lodging, and reduced yield.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3d
   <<decision>>: Is the pest stink bug, armyworm, cutworm, stalk borer, or wheat stem maggot with significant infestation?
     <<if yes>>: Implement control measures appropriate to the specific pest and severity level.
     <<if no>>: Monitor and reassess if conditions change.

<<end>>

9b484270.trigger: When adult flies (pale green to yellow with dark stripes, ~6 mm) are observed in wheat fields, or when symptoms of stem girdling, premature yellowing of heads, shriveled grain, or lodging are detected.
9b484270.content:
<<trigger>>: When adult flies (pale green to yellow with dark stripes, ~6 mm) are observed in wheat fields, or when symptoms of stem girdling, premature yellowing of heads, shriveled grain, or lodging are detected.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the pest based on symptoms and life cycle characteristics.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms premature yellowing of the head, shriveled grain, stem girdling, and lodging, with adults appearing from late spring to midsummer?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed with sawfly (Cephus cinctus) management: note that fall-sown cereals are more commonly attacked and wheat lines with solid or partially solid stems are less susceptible; monitor for discontinuous infestations.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Assess if damage includes wilting/dying patches at seedling stage, with roots partially or completely severed.
   <<decision>>: Are stunted patches observed, and when soil is examined, are large larvae (up to several cm long, ~1 cm thick, with three pairs of legs on thorax) found?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as white grubs (May/June beetle larvae). Avoid seeding wheat into heavily infested grasslands; note that damage may be non-uniform and plants may survive if roots not completely destroyed.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Check for wireworm damage: wilting/dying of adjacent plants in rows or patches, stems chewed just above the seed, and seed coats left after endosperm eaten.
   <<decision>>: Are tough, wire-like larvae (20-30 mm long, smooth, hard, polished, with three pairs of legs, color cream to brown) found in association with damaged seedlings?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as wireworms (click beetle larvae). Note that damage is most severe where wheat is seeded after fallow or after several years of grass; generations overlap so all sizes may be present.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Evaluate for slugs, snails, grasshoppers, or crickets: look for feeding on endosperm of germinating seed, seedlings bitten off at ground level, or longitudinal stripes chewed on leaves giving frayed appearance.
   <<decision>>: Are slugs, snails, grasshoppers, or crickets observed causing such damage?
     <<if yes>>: Note that these pests are usually localized but can cause great damage to individual wheat stands; monitor and manage accordingly.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
5. Inspect for mites: look for silvery flecking on leaves, webs, stunting, poor heading, or whitening of plants. Use magnification to detect very small mites (<1 mm) with four pairs of legs (adults) or two pairs (wheat curl mite, Eriophyes tulipae).
   <<decision>>: Are mites present in large numbers causing these symptoms?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as mite infestation; note that mites are not insects and have sucking mouthparts; manage based on species.
     <<if no>>: Re-evaluate field for other causes or consult further diagnostic resources.
<<end>>

b5b39df7.trigger: When a leaf sample shows potential mite infestation but no visible mites are detected with the unaided eye.
b5b39df7.content:
<<trigger>>: When a leaf sample shows potential mite infestation but no visible mites are detected with the unaided eye.
<<steps>>:
1. Hold the infested leaf over a piece of white paper folded to form a trough.
   <<decision>>: Is the leaf tapped sharply several times?
     <<if yes>>: Observe whether hundreds of mites fall onto the paper and are seen moving about.
     <<if no>>: Repeat tapping until mites are dislodged or confirm absence.
<<end>>

2ec43a48.trigger: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of poor growth, discoloration, or necrosis that may be due to mineral deficiencies, toxicities, or environmental stresses.
2ec43a48.content:
<<trigger>>: When a wheat crop shows symptoms of poor growth, discoloration, or necrosis that may be due to mineral deficiencies, toxicities, or environmental stresses.
<<steps>>:
1. Assess visual symptoms and field conditions to determine the likely cause.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms uniform across the field?
     <<if yes>>: Proceed to step 2 (likely genetic or systemic issue).
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3 (likely environmental or soil-related issue).
2. Evaluate for genetic disorders (genetic flecking, hybrid necrosis, melanism).
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms chlorotic flecking or blotching, especially on later-stage spring wheat, without yield loss?
     <<if yes>>: Identify as genetic flecking; no action needed unless severe necrosis appears.
     <<if no>>: Check for hybrid necrosis (necrosis with stunting/dwarf clumping in early generation material); if present, eliminate affected progeny.
3. Check for nutrient deficiencies.
   <<decision>>: Are lower leaves pale green to yellow, starting from tip to sheath?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect nitrogen deficiency; apply nitrogen fertilizer as needed.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to sub-step 3a.
   3a. <<decision>>: Are plants stunted with fewer shoots, and lower leaves pale to yellowish-red with possible purple culm bases?
       <<if yes>>: Suspect phosphorus deficiency; apply phosphorus fertilizer as needed.
       <<if no>>: Proceed to sub-step 3b.
   3b. <<decision>>: Are lower leaf tips and margins dry and scorched with shortened internodes?
       <<if yes>>: Suspect potassium deficiency; apply potassium fertilizer as needed.
       <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Check for micronutrient deficiencies.
   <<decision>>: Are there grayish necrotic spots/streaks on basal portion of newest leaves, with possible kinking/twisting?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect manganese deficiency; apply foliar manganese sulfate.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to sub-step 4a.
   4a. <<decision>>: Are young leaf tips discolored, breaking, curling, with bleached/sterile spikes or poor spike emergence?
       <<if yes>>: Suspect copper deficiency; apply copper fertilizer as needed.
       <<if no>>: Proceed to step 5.
5. Check for toxicity or environmental stress.
   <<decision>>: Are roots stubby and brown, with small leaves, shortened internodes, and leaf tip death, especially in low pH soil?
     <<if yes>>: Suspect aluminum toxicity; reduce toxicity by liming.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to sub-step 5a.
   5a. <<decision>>: Is crop growth variable within the field with barren spots, stunted dark blue-green plants, and tip burn on leaf margins?
       <<if yes>>: Suspect salt stress; confirm with soil test; if excessive, manage irrigation and drainage.
       <<if no>>: Proceed to sub-step 5b.
   5b. <<decision>>: Are plants stunted with reduced tillering, leaf curling/rolling during midday, or spikelet/floret reduction, especially during booting or seed set?
       <<if yes>>: Suspect moisture stress; manage irrigation to avoid critical period stress.
       <<if no>>: Proceed to sub-step 5c.
   5c. <<decision>>: Are symptoms associated with high temperatures (increased development rate, reduced growth)?
       <<if yes>>: Suspect heat stress; manage as for moisture stress and consider shading or timing adjustments.
       <<if no>>: Re-evaluate for combined stresses or other causes not listed.
<<end>>

48e6d766.trigger: When high temperatures or frost damage is suspected in wheat crops, or when herbicide phytotoxicity from 2,4-D or triazine residues is observed.
48e6d766.content:
<<trigger>>: When high temperatures or frost damage is suspected in wheat crops, or when herbicide phytotoxicity from 2,4-D or triazine residues is observed.
<<steps>>:
1. Identify the type of damage based on symptoms and timing.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms leaf curling, deformed spikes, or sterility near anthesis?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute to 2,4-D herbicide application too early or near anthesis; note that deformations seldom cause significant losses in small grain cereals.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 2.
2. Assess for triazine herbicide residue damage.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms leaf bleaching followed by necrosis?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute to triazine (e.g., atrazine) residues from previous crop; note that damage results from excessive amounts, wrong growth stage, or wrong species.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 3.
3. Evaluate for frost damage.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms chlorosis, banding/striping on leaves or spikes, bleached white tissue, sterility at flowering, or separated peduncle epidermis?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute to frost; note that young/newly emerged tissue and flowering parts are most susceptible, and frost can be serious if late in crop cycle.
     <<if no>>: Proceed to step 4.
4. Assess for high temperature damage.
   <<decision>>: Are symptoms reduced spikelets, florets, grain filling, or plant death from protein denaturation, especially during late-boot, seed-set, or flowering to maturity stages, possibly with desiccating winds?
     <<if yes>>: Attribute to high temperatures; note that very high temperatures can kill plants, and major yield reductions may occur if combined with hot, dry winds.
     <<if no>>: Conclude that damage is not from these specific causes; consider other factors not covered in this document.
<<end>>
